{centering}Tests of restricted quantum focusing and a new CFT bound

Victor Franken12** * victor.franken@ugent.be, Sami Kaya3†† † samikaya@berkeley.edu, François Rondeau4‡‡ ‡ francois.rondeau@ens-lyon.fr, Arvin Shahbazi-Moghaddam35§§ § arvinshm@gmail.com and Patrick Tran3¶¶ ¶ patrick.tran@berkeley.edu

1 CPHT, CNRS, Ecole polytechnique, Institut Polytechnique de Paris
91120 Palaiseau, France

Abstract

The restricted quantum focusing conjecture (rQFC) plays a central role in an axiomatic formulation of semiclassical gravity. Since much hinges on its validity, it is imperative to subject the rQFC to rigorous tests in novel settings. Here we do so in two independent directions.

First, we prove rQFC in a class of spacetime dimension d=2d=2 toy models, JT gravity coupled to a QFT. We also construct explicit counter-examples to the original and stronger Quantum Focusing Conjecture in a regime where matter quantum effects are comparable to the total dilaton value.

Second, for d>2d>2, we derive from the rQFC a constraint stronger than the Quantum Null Energy Condition (QNEC). In a broad class of states, this bound forbids the QNEC from saturating faster than O⁡(𝒜)O(\mathcal{A}) as the transverse area 𝒜\mathcal{A} of a certain null deformation shrinks to zero. We speculate about a universal strengthened QNEC holding across all QFT states.

1 Introduction

Semiclassical gravity is believed to emerge from a fundamental theory of quantum gravity. To learn about this fundamental theory, a powerful strategy is to find imprints of its basic principles in the semiclassical limit. Take, for example, the principle of independence between different fundamental subsystems. In Anti-de Sitter (AdS)/Conformal Field Theory (CFT) correspondence, where fundamental theory is the boundary CFT on some Lorentzian manifold, spacelike separated domains of dependence are independent. The semiclassical imprint of this in AdS is that the gravity duals of the boundary domains of dependence must also be spacelike separated. This gravity constraint was in turn shown to follow from a deeper quantum gravity constraint called the quantum focusing conjecture (QFC).

The QFC was first proposed in [16] and has since been crucially used in proofs of many significant results in AdS/CFT, including the above-mentioned “entanglement wedge nesting” (see e.g., [5, 3, 20, 30, 53, 29, 18]). Beyond AdS/CFT, the QFC implies the generalized second law (GSL) [11, 16], quantum singularity theorems [73, 17, 19], and the existence of quantum extremal surfaces [31, 5, 4], leading in particular to a resolution of the black hole information problem [58, 7]. The QFC also implies the Quantum Null Energy Condition (QNEC), a bound in Quantum Field Theory (QFT) which was then proved with various different QFT techniques [15, 48, 3, 10, 23, 44].

To state the QFC, let us first introduce its main ingredient, the generalized entropy SgenS_{\text{gen}}, a sort of entropy of spacetime regions [12]. Let 𝒲\mathcal{W} denote a spacetime wedge (i.e., a domain of dependence of a partial Cauchy slice) in a general spacetime. In perturbative quantum (Einstein) gravity, the generalized entropy of 𝒲\mathcal{W} is schematically given by:

Sgen​(𝒲)=A⁡(ð​𝒲)4​G+Sren​(𝒲)+⋯,\displaystyle S_{\text{gen}}(\mathcal{W})=\frac{A(\eth\mathcal{W})}{4G}+S_{\rm ren}(\mathcal{W})+\cdots, (1.1)

where A⁡(ð​𝒲)A(\eth\mathcal{W}) denotes the area of the edge of 𝒲\mathcal{W}, defined as ð​𝒲=∂+𝒲∩∂−𝒲\eth\mathcal{W}=\partial^{+}\mathcal{W}\cap\partial^{-}\mathcal{W} where ∂±𝒲\partial^{\pm}\mathcal{W} denote the future/past sections of ∂𝒲\partial\mathcal{W}, the boundary of 𝒲\mathcal{W} (see Fig. 1), and Sren​(𝒲)S_{\rm ren}(\mathcal{W}) denotes the renormalized von Neumann entropy of the fields in 𝒲\mathcal{W}. In fact, the complete generalized entropy functional involves more terms than in Eq. (1.1). Later on, in Sec. 2, we will discuss the complete expansion of SgenS_{\rm gen} in the context of semiclassical gravity.

The QFC constrains the variations of SgenS_{\text{gen}} under certain deformations of 𝒲\mathcal{W}. In particular, let us deform the wedge by translating ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} in a neighborhood of a point on ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} along the null generators of ∂+𝒲\partial^{+}\mathcal{W} (which emanate orthogonally from ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W}) by an affine parameter amount V⁡(ya)V(y^{a}), where yay^{a} denotes coordinates for the transverse direction ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W}, so a∈{1,⋯,d−2}a\in\{1,\cdots,d-2\} where dd denotes spacetime dimensionality.

The quantum expansion of any wedge in this V⁡(ya)V(y^{a})-labeled family is a function Θ|𝒲:ð𝒲→ℝ\left.\Theta\right\rvert_{\mathcal{W}}:\eth\mathcal{W}\to\mathbb{R} defined by

Θ|𝒲(ya)=4​Ghδ​Sgenδ​V​(ya),\displaystyle\left.\Theta\right\rvert_{\mathcal{W}}(y^{a})=\frac{4G}{\sqrt{h}}\frac{\delta S_{\text{gen}}}{\delta V(y^{a})}, (1.2)

where hh denotes the determinant of the intrinsic metric of ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} [16].11 1 We suppose here that V⁡(ya)V(y^{a}) is small enough that one does not encounter caustics along ∂+𝒲\partial^{+}\mathcal{W}. This can always be arranged for smooth ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} which we restrict to for the rest of this paper.

Let us now define a 11-parameter family of wedges 𝒲λ\mathcal{W}_{\lambda} by Vλ​(ya)V_{\lambda}(y^{a}) such that ∂λVλ​(ya)≥0\partial_{\lambda}V_{\lambda}(y^{a})\geq 0. The QFC is then the following constraint:

∂λΘλ≤0,\displaystyle\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}\leq 0, (1.3)

where the notation Θλ\Theta_{\lambda} will be our shorthand for Θ|𝒲λ\left.\Theta\right\rvert_{\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}}. Note that the QFC demands Eq. (1.3) on all of ð​𝒲λ\eth{\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}}.

Despite its central role in quantum gravity, the QFC has not been proven. In [63], a weaker constraint called the restricted quantum focusing conjecture (rQFC) was put forth. The rQFC states:

∂λΘλ​(ya)≤0,at λ and ya∈ð​𝒲λ such that Θλ​(ya)=0.\displaystyle\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})\leq 0,~~~~\text{at $\lambda$ and $y^{a}\in\eth\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}$ such that $\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=0$}. (1.4)

Even though rQFC is weaker than the QFC, it was argued in [63] that it implies all crucial known implications of the QFC, including the ones mentioned above.22 2 This is because, so far, in all applications only the following implication of the QFC is used: Θλ1≤0⟹Θλ2≤0,if ​λ1≤λ2,\displaystyle\Theta_{\lambda_{1}}\leq 0\implies\Theta_{\lambda_{2}}\leq 0,\qquad\text{if }\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}, (1.5) where Θλ≤0\Theta_{\lambda}\leq 0 means everywhere in the transverse direction ð​𝒲λ\eth\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}. Quite generically, a violation of Eq. (1.5) implies the existence of a λ\lambda between λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2}, at which Eq. (1.4) is violated. Highly non-generic cases (e.g., Θλ=λ3\Theta_{\lambda}=\lambda^{3}, where ∂λΘλ=∂λ2Θλ=0\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}=\partial_{\lambda}^{2}\Theta_{\lambda}=0 at λ=0\lambda=0) naively evades this argument as it satisfies Eq. (1.4) but not Eq. (1.5). We believe that these non-generic examples are also disallowed since otherwise a slight perturbation to these spacetimes, or even to the family Vλ​(ya)V_{\lambda}(y^{a}) will bring back genericity and would violate Eq. (1.4). To skip this subtlety entirely, one can define rQFC to be the statement of Eq. (1.5), as was done for example in [6, 18]. We thank Raphael Bousso and Edward Witten for bringing up this non-generic case to our attention. Furthermore, the rQFC was proved in [63] in a class of semiclassical gravity theories, the so-called holographic braneworld models [60, 61, 64, 39, 70, 46, 28, 55].33 3 The proof strategy in [63] is not obviously generalizable to a proof of ∂λΘλ≤0\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}\leq 0. The rQFC has since been adopted as a central piece of an axiomatic framework of semiclassical gravity [18, 6]. We therefore find it necessary to put the rQFC to new tests, to both check its validity and learn new things from it. Along these lines, we can ask two natural questions:

  • •

    Does the rQFC hold in all reasonable theories? And, are there violations of the (original) QFC, especially as its crucial known implications appear to simply follow from the weaker rQFC?

  • •

    Can we predict novel QFT constraints from the rQFC? (A direct proof of which would then constitute non-trivial evidence for the rQFC.)

This paper is motivated by these questions. In particular, in Sec. 3 we prove the rQFC in a class of d=2d=2 toy models, Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity coupled to a QFT. We then find explicit counter-examples to the original QFC in this model. The violations occur in a regime where we do not know of a dimensional reduction interpretation of the toy model, and must therefore be understood strictly within the toy model. Consequently, we do not hold this as very convincing evidence against the QFC. It is remarkable, however, that the rQFC seems to be robust enough to hold in that regime. In Sec. 4, we focus on d>2d>2, and show that a new G→0G\to 0 limit of the rQFC, one in which we simultaneosly send the width of the null deformation profile to zero, implies a novel CFT constraint. As we review below, the standard G→0G\to 0 limit was used to extract the QNEC. In the class of states we consider, the novel constraints are indeed stronger than the QNEC.

Before summarizing these results in more detail, let us say that the above-mentioned definitions of QFC/rQFC for general 𝒲\mathcal{W} require the existence of a classical background metric.44 4 It is conceivable that the requirement of an exactly classical metric can be relaxed, at least for certain region such as exteriors (or interior) of event horizons. And therefore our use of the semiclassical regime is more for caution than necessity. See Sec. 2 for a discussion. In order to obtain a classical background at a level of approximation in which quantum corrections from the matter sector are important in the generalized entropy, a standard approach is to consider a semiclassical gravity regime 55 5 So far in the introduction, as in much of the literature, the term semiclassical gravity was used vaguely. Here, and in Sec. 2 we attempt to clarify our use of the term in this paper. in which large number of matter fields cc are present and one takes the limit:

G→0,c​G≡ℓSd−2=fixed,\displaystyle G\to 0,~~cG\equiv\ell_{S}^{d-2}=\text{fixed}, (1.6)

where we call the scale ℓS\ell_{S} controlling the backreaction the species scale. This regime in effect suppresses quantum corrections from gravitons compared to those from the matter sector, making it possible to approximate the spacetime as classical and backreacting to ⟨Ti​j⟩\langle T_{ij}\rangle, the expectation value of the stress-energy tensor.

Given our use of the semiclassical regime, we will review it in more detail in Sec. 2. In the rest of this section, we will summarize the main results of this paper, which are divided into two separate and self-contained sections 3 and 4.

Results in d=2d=2 toy model: rQFC proof and QFC counter-example

In Sec. 3, we investigate the validity of the QFC and rQFC in JT gravity coupled to a two-dimensional QFT with large number of species in the semiclassical regime (1.6).66 6 Even though this model arises approximately as a dimensional reduction of higher dimensional gravity theories, we treat it as an exact d=2d=2 toy model, and do not focus on any higher dimensional interpretation, except for some sporadic remarks. In this theory, we define the quantum expansion as:

Θλ=4​GΦ​∂λSgen.\displaystyle\Theta_{\lambda}=\frac{4G}{\Phi}\partial_{\lambda}S_{\text{gen}}. (1.7)

This definition is informed by the more general definition in Eq. (1.2), where we have replaced the transverse area factor h\sqrt{h} with its JT gravity counterpart, the dilaton Φ\Phi.77 7 See Appendix A for a review of this dictionary.

In this model, the rQFC follows from the QNEC, which we will discuss in a moment, and which was proven in QFT in [15, 48, 10, 23, 44], as well as in two-dimensional CFTs in [8]. Taking the derivative of Θλ\Theta_{\lambda} and using the QNEC, we find

∂λΘλ≤−θλ​Θλ,\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}\leq-\theta_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}, (1.8)

where θλ=∂λlog⁡Φ\theta_{\lambda}=\partial_{\lambda}\log\Phi. It follows that

Θλ=0⇒∂λΘλ≤0.\Theta_{\lambda}=0\hskip 10.00002pt\Rightarrow\hskip 10.00002pt\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}\leq 0. (1.9)

This shows that the rQFC holds while allowing for QFC violations when θλ​Θλ<0\theta_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}<0. It might be naively tempting to say that the bound (1.8) which is stronger than rQFC but not equivalent to the QFC holds in quantum gravity in general dimensions. This is false, however, since the bound in the classical regime amounts to ∂λ2(Area)≤0\partial_{\lambda}^{2}(\text{Area})\leq 0 and is therefore violated by a lightcone in Minkowski spacetime whose cross sectional area, say in d=4d=4, satisfies Area=4​π​λ2\text{Area}=4\pi\lambda^{2}.

The central part of our rQFC proof is the use of the two-dimensional QNEC. This proof strategy is identical to the work of Almheiri-Mahajan-Maldacena (AMM) in [8], and in that sense it is not original. There is, however, a crucial distinction between the interpretation of our results. AMM present their work as a proof of the QFC, whereas we derive the rQFC. The discrepancy between the claims stems from the fact that AMM define quantum expansion without the factor of Φ\Phi in the denominator in Eq. (1.7), a choice which breaks with the original definition of the quantum expansion which is used in defining the QFC. With the proper definition (Eq. (1.7)), their proof simply reduces to ours, as we present in Sec. 3.

In the remainder of Sec. 3, we study explicit scenarios in our toy model with negative and positive cosmological constant and find explicit violations of the QFC (Eq. (1.2)). We briefly assess the regimes and regions where we should look for such violations. The bound (1.8) shows that counter-examples can only appear in regions where matter quantum effects are competing with the scale of the dilaton (ℓS=c​G≳Φ\ell_{S}=cG\gtrsim\Phi). Intuitively, the sufficient condition θλ​Θλ<0\theta_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}<0 implies that the variation of matter entropy is strong enough to switch the direction of quantum expansion compared to the direction of geometric expansion. Such regions exist close to evaporating horizons.

Motivated by this observation, we study the near-horizon regions of an AdS extremal black hole and of an evaporating cosmological horizon in de Sitter spacetime. In particular, we construct these backgrounds in JT gravity coupled to a CFT. Using a strong version of the QNEC derived in [72], one can show that violations only appear if the species scale c​GcG is of the order or greater than the dilaton Φ\Phi, that is, if the quantum effects of matter on the quantum expansion are allowed to compete with the geometric terms. In this regime, we then explicitly find large subregions where θλ​Θλ<0\theta_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}<0, and for which the QFC is indeed violated.

This is a regime where JT gravity does not admit a higher dimensional uplift, and is therefore in a true sense a toy model. We therefore do not interpret this as strong evidence against the original QFC.

Results in d>2d>2: rQFC implies a new CFT bound

In Sec. 4, we show that in a class of near-vacuum states, the rQFC implies a new CFT bound. This is a new instance of quantum gravity constraints predicting QFT constraints. A well-known previous example is the QNEC, which was originally derived in [16] from the QFC, and subsequently proved in several papers [15, 48, 10, 23, 44]. The new CFT bound is stronger than the QNEC.

Let us demonstrate how the QNEC is implied by the rQFC.88 8 As opposed to the QFC, which is an unnecessarily stronger condition for this purpose. This will set the stage for the above-mentioned new CFT constraint. Here, we will work with the schematic form of the generalized entropy in Eq. (1.1), namely just the area and the renormalized entropy term. In Sec. 4 we will be more careful and reproduce the main results using a more careful ansatz of the perturbative semiclassical regime (see Sec. 2), including the subleading corrections which will be omitted here. From Eq. (1.1), we obtain

Θλ=θλ+4​Ghλδ​Srenδ​V​(ya)|λ+⋯,\displaystyle\Theta_{\lambda}=\theta_{\lambda}+\frac{4G}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}+\cdots, (1.10)

where θλ=∂λlog⁡hλ\theta_{\lambda}=\partial_{\lambda}\log\sqrt{h_{\lambda}} (where hλh_{\lambda} is the determinant of the intrinsic metric of ð​𝒲λ\eth\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}) is the classical expansion of the VλV_{\lambda} congruence. The ellipsis here and in the rest of this section is there to indicate we are dropping corrections, keeping only terms that we claim will be relevant for the argument.

We can now take another λ\lambda derivative of Eq. (1.10) to obtain:

∂λΘλ\displaystyle\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda} =−θλ2d−2−ςλ2−Ri​jkikj−4​G​θλhλδ​Srenδ​V​(ya)|λ+4​Ghλ∂λδ​Srenδ​V​(ya)|λ+⋯,\displaystyle=-\frac{\theta_{\lambda}^{2}}{d-2}-\varsigma_{\lambda}^{2}-R_{ij}k^{i}k^{j}-\frac{4G\theta_{\lambda}}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}+\frac{4G}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}+\cdots, (1.11)

where ςλ2\varsigma_{\lambda}^{2} is the shear-squared of ∂+𝒲\partial^{+}\mathcal{W}. The first three terms on the RHS of Eq. (1.11) equal ∂λθλ\partial_{\lambda}\theta_{\lambda} through the Raychaudhuri’s equation for the affine (surface-orthogonal) congruence VλV_{\lambda}. The last two terms in Eq. (1.11) both come from the λ\lambda derivative of the second term in Eq. (1.10).

Now, consider a QFT state in d>2d>2 Minkowski spacetime, and let 𝒲λ\mathcal{W}_{\lambda} be a null-deformed family starting from the domain of dependence of a ball-shaped region.99 9 More precisely, we mean that the wedge 𝒲\mathcal{W} approaches the domain of dependence of a ball-shaped region in the G→0G\to 0 limit. For a general state, the region will get perturbatively distorted away from this. The spacetime will in general backreact to the state, in particular, through the following component of Einstein field equations:

Ri​j​ki​kj=8​π​G​⟨Ti​j⟩​ki​kj,\displaystyle R_{ij}k^{i}k^{j}=8\pi G\langle T_{ij}\rangle k^{i}k^{j}, (1.12)

where ⟨Ti​j⟩\langle T_{ij}\rangle is the expectation value of the stress-energy tensor, and kik^{i} is any null vector.1010 10 Coupling the expectation value ⟨Ti​j⟩\langle T_{ij}\rangle to the classical field Ri​jR_{ij} is justified in the semiclassical gravity regime (1.6).

Next, we impose the rQFC condition Θλ​(ya)=0\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=0 at some point ya∈ð​𝒲y^{a}\in\eth\mathcal{W}, perturbatively in GG:

Θλ(ya)=0⟹θλ(ya)=−4​Ghλδ​Srenδ​V​(ya)|λ+⋯.\displaystyle\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=0\implies\theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=-\frac{4G}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}+\cdots. (1.13)

This enforces the (un-backreacted) size of the ball RR to scale with GG, because θλ∼R−1\theta_{\lambda}\sim R^{-1}.

Finally, by combining Eqs. (1.11), (1.12), and (1.13), we get:

Θλ​(ya)=0⟹∂λΘλ​(ya)=16​(d−3)​G2(d−2)(1hλδ​Srenδ​V​(ya)|λ)2−4G(2π⟨Ti​j⟩kikj−1hλ∂λδ​Srenδ​V​(ya)|λ)+⋯,\begin{split}\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=0\implies\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=&\,\frac{16(d-3)G^{2}}{(d-2)}\left(\left.\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}\right)^{2}\\ &-4G\left(2\pi\langle T_{ij}\rangle k^{i}k^{j}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}\right)+\cdots,\end{split} (1.14)

where kik^{i} is the (surface-orthogonal) null vector field on ∂+𝒲\partial^{+}\mathcal{W} which generates the Vλ​(ya)V_{\lambda}(y^{a}) flow. Note that since the shear of the ∂+𝒲\partial^{+}\mathcal{W} congruence is zero in Minkowski spacetime, and the perturbation to Minkowski space is O⁡(G)O(G), therefore the shear-squared term in Eq. (1.11) is O⁡(G2)O(G^{2}).

Demanding the non-positivity of ∂λΘλ\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda} in Eq. (1.14) is a re-statement of the gravitational constraint rQFC.1111 11 The expression in Eq.(1.14) was referred to in [13], as an improved QNEC. However, the standard G→0G\to 0 simply yields the previously known QNEC. However, by dividing the RHS of Eq. (1.14) by GG and taking the G→0G\to 0 limit, the ball-shaped region limit to the Rindler wedge (since the ball radius OPENR∼θλ−1∼G−1)R\sim\theta_{\lambda}^{-1}\sim G^{-1}), and we obtain the QNEC as a pure QFT constraint. Explicitly,

2π⟨Ti​j⟩kikj−1hλ∂λδ​Srenδ​V​(ya)|λ≥0,\displaystyle 2\pi\langle T_{ij}\rangle k^{i}k^{j}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}\geq 0, (1.15)

for 𝒲λ\mathcal{W}_{\lambda} null deformation of a Rindler wedge 1212 12 The QNEC can also be derived on an arbitrary curved background from the QFC [16] (and we expect also from the rQFC), subject to the local conditions θλ=ςλ2=0\theta_{\lambda}=\varsigma^{2}_{\lambda}=0. Here, for simplicity we concentrate on the case of Minkowski space and the Rindler wedge, which in particular satisfies those conditions.. Here, ⟨Ti​j⟩\langle T_{ij}\rangle is being evaluate at yay^{a} on ð​𝒲λ\eth\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}. 1313 13 Though we only focus on the Rindler wedge case here, one can define QNEC in curved spacetime as well, and we expect that to follow from the rQFC as well. The d>2d>2 QNEC in curved spacetime was proved for holographic CFTs in [3].

So far, we have shown that a standard G→0G\to 0 limit of Eq. (1.14) leads to the QNEC. Let us now introduce a parameter Σ\Sigma which controls the transverse length scale of the null deformation profile Vλ​(ya)V_{\lambda}(y^{a}). For instance, we can take Vλ​(ya)V_{\lambda}(y^{a}) to be λ\lambda times a bump function with characteristic width Σ\Sigma:

Vλ​(ya)=λ​exp⁡[11−Σ2/|y|2],|y|≤Σ,\displaystyle V_{\lambda}(y^{a})=\lambda~\exp\left[\frac{1}{1-\Sigma^{2}/|y|^{2}}\right],~~~~~~~|y|\leq\Sigma, (1.16)

where |y||y| denotes proper distance on ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W}.

In Sec. 4, we find that a different G→0G\to 0 limit of the rQFC, one in which we simultaneously send Σ→0\Sigma\to 0 while keeping Σd−2≫G\Sigma^{d-2}\gg G (as required for validity of perturbation theory) gives a new (stronger) bound on CFTs.1414 14 For instance, let Σ=L1−α​Gαd−2\Sigma=L^{1-\alpha}G^{\frac{\alpha}{d-2}} for 0<α<10<\alpha<1, where LL is some large scale associated to the state under consideration. This is because the limit creates a competition between the first and the second lines on the RHS of ∂λΘλ\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda} in Eq. (1.14). We work this out explicitly in a class of near-vacuum states where we have a lot of computational control over the terms in Eq. (1.14). We sketch the basic idea and main results in the rest of this section, and we also speculate about a more general stronger-than-QNEC bound.

First, we use a conformal transformation to map the null-deformed ball-shaped regions 𝒲λ\mathcal{W}_{\lambda} to null-deformed Rindler wedges 𝒲~λ\tilde{\mathcal{W}}_{\lambda}. In a CFT, we can use this to relate the second line of Eq. (1.14) to its counter-part on the Rindler wedge. It turns out that:

2π⟨Ti​j⟩kikj−1hλ∂λδ​Srenδ​V​(ya)|λ−1hλ2​θλd−2δ​Srenδ​V​(ya)|λ=2π⟨T~i​j⟩k~ik~j−1h~λ∂λδ​S~renδ​V~​(y~a)|λ,\displaystyle 2\pi\langle T_{ij}\rangle k^{i}k^{j}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\frac{2\theta_{\lambda}}{d-2}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}=2\pi\langle\tilde{T}_{ij}\rangle\tilde{k}^{i}\tilde{k}^{j}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{h}_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}, (1.17)

where the tilded quantities denote the analogous of the LHS quantities but pertaining to a Rindler wedge 𝒲~\tilde{\mathcal{W}}. The wedge 𝒲~λ\tilde{\mathcal{W}}_{\lambda} is then determined by the function v~=V~​(y~a)\tilde{v}=\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a}). The (extra) third term on the LHS of Eq. (1.17) comes from a non-linear relationship between Vλ​(ya)V_{\lambda}(y^{a}) and V~λ​(y~a)\tilde{V}_{\lambda}(\tilde{y}^{a}).

We can combine Eq. (1.17) with Eq. (1.14), to obtain:

Θλ​(ya)=0⟹∂λΘλ​(ya)\displaystyle\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=0\implies\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a}) =16​(d−1)d−2G2(1hλδ​Srenδ​V​(ya)|λ)2\displaystyle=\frac{16(d-1)}{d-2}G^{2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}\right)^{2}
−4G(2π⟨T~i​j⟩k~ik~j−1h~λ∂λδ​S~renδ​V~​(y~a)|λ)+⋯.\displaystyle-4G\left(2\pi\langle\tilde{T}_{ij}\rangle\tilde{k}^{i}\tilde{k}^{j}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{h}_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}\right)+\cdots. (1.18)

It turns out that for a generic class of near-vacuum states:1515 15 The near-vacuum states are chosen for simplicity of the analysis in Sec. 4 to have no stress-energy tensor in the vicinity of the deformation profile.

|ψ⟩=|0⟩+i​ϵ​|χ⟩+O⁡(ϵ2),\displaystyle\ket{\psi}=\ket{0}+i\epsilon\ket{\chi}+O(\epsilon^{2}), (1.19)

the Rindler wedge quantity on the second line of Eq. (1.18) can be computed explicitly [9] (see also [51], and Appendix B for a review). In particular, a non-trivial scaling with Σ\Sigma as Σ→0\Sigma\to 0 can be obtained:

2π⟨T~i​j⟩k~ik~j−1h~λ∂λδ​S~renδ​V~​(y~a)|λ=O(ϵ2Σd−2−δ)\displaystyle 2\pi\langle\tilde{T}_{ij}\rangle\tilde{k}^{i}\tilde{k}^{j}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{h}_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}=O(\epsilon^{2}\Sigma^{d-2-\delta}) (1.20)

where δ\delta depends on both the theory and the state. We will discuss it in more detail below. 1h~λδ​S~renδ​V~​(y~a)|λ=O(ϵ),\displaystyle\left.\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{h}_{\lambda}}}\frac{\delta\tilde{S}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}=O(\epsilon), (1.21)

Let us discuss how Eqs. (1.18), (1.20), and (1.21) result in a bound stronger than the QNEC. As explained, the regular G→0G\to 0 limit of Eq. (1.18) yields the QNEC. The conclusion is that an appropriate G,Σ→0G,\Sigma\to 0 limit of the rQFC implies the following stronger-than-QNEC bound in all CFTs:

1h~λδ​S~renδ​V~​(y~a)|λ=O(ϵ)⟹2π⟨T~i​j⟩k~ik~j−1h~λ∂λδ​S~renδ​V~​(y~a)|λ≥Σ→0O(ϵ2Σd−2)≥0,\displaystyle\left.\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{h}_{\lambda}}}\frac{\delta\tilde{S}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}=O(\epsilon)\implies 2\pi\langle\tilde{T}_{ij}\rangle\tilde{k}^{i}\tilde{k}^{j}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{h}_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Sigma\to 0}}{{\geq}}O(\epsilon^{2}\Sigma^{d-2})\geq 0, (1.23)

In particular, this bound is stronger than the QNEC applied to this state, which only demands that the LHS of Eq. (1.20) is positive.

Let us now comment on the origin of the parameter δ\delta in Eq. (1.20). In [9], it was found that δ\delta in Eq.(1.20) can be obtained from the following:

∫−∞∞d​s​⟨χs|​ℰ​(y~a)\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}ds\bra{\chi_s}\mathcal{E}(\tilde{y}^{a}) OPENℰ⁡(y~′a)​|χs⟩=y~→y~′O​(|y~−y~′|)−δ),\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\tilde{y}^{\prime a})\ket{\chi_s}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{y}\to\tilde{y}^{\prime}}}{{=}}O(|\tilde{y}-\tilde{y}^{\prime}|)^{-\delta}),
where,​ℰ​(y~a)=\displaystyle\text{where,}~~~\mathcal{E}(\tilde{y}^{a})= ∫−∞∞d​v~​Ti​j​(v~,y~a)​k~i​k~j.\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\tilde{v}~T_{ij}(\tilde{v},\tilde{y}^{a})\tilde{k}^{i}\tilde{k}^{j}. (1.24)
