|χs⟩=e−i​K​s​|χ⟩\displaystyle\ket{\chi_s}=e^{-iKs}\ket{\chi} (1.25)

where KK is the boost generator around the Rindler wedge. In Appendix D, we analyze the rQFC implication that δ≥0\delta\geq 0 from the perspective of the operator product expansion of ℰ\mathcal{E}’s.

We can summarize the story so far in the following diagram:

Let us end the introduction with a speculation. Our new CFT bound (1.23) is stronger than the QNEC in the particular class of near-vacuum states (1.19). But it is unsatisfactory to only have such a bound in this limited regime. It is natural to expect that, in fact, a universal (holding in all QFTs in all states) stronger-than-QNEC bound is true. In the Σ→0\Sigma\to 0 regime, this bound would presumably prevent the QNEC from scaling with Σα\Sigma^{\alpha} with α>d−2\alpha>d-2, whenever δ​Sren/δ​V​(ya)≠0\delta S_{\rm ren}/\delta V(y^{a})\neq 0. These conditions can culminate in the following natural bound for null deformations of the Rindler wedge:

2π⟨Ti​j⟩kikj−1hλ∂λδ​Srenδ​V​(ya)|λ≥Σ→0κΣd−2(1hλδ​Srenδ​V​(ya)|λ)2,(Speculative)\displaystyle 2\pi\langle T_{ij}\rangle k^{i}k^{j}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Sigma\to 0}}{{\geq}}\kappa\Sigma^{d-2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}\right)^{2},~~~~~~\text{(Speculative)} (1.26)

where κ>0\kappa>0 is to be determined. This bound would then hold by either the LHS scaling with Σα\Sigma^{\alpha} as Σ→0\Sigma\to 0 for 0≤α<d−20\leq\alpha<d-2, or with α=d−2\alpha=d-2 in which case the competition of magnitudes between LHS and RHS becomes non-trivial. The bound (1.26) is reminiscent of the d=2d=2 strengthened QNEC in CFTs, which was proposed in [72], and proved in general states in [8]. We leave an exploration of this bound to future work.

2 Review of the semiclassical gravity regime

In this section, we give a brief review of the semiclassical gravity regime which we employ in this paper. Since this is just an overview of basics, readers who feel confident about what is meant by the regime (1.6), and the resulting action, and generalized entropy functional, can skip ahead to the next sections. See [34] and some references within for a more extensive discussion of the semiclassical gravity regime, including some technical challenges, and some of their proposed resolutions.

As mentioned in the introduction, our definitions of the quantum expansion Θ\Theta in Eq. (1.2) (and therefore the QFC and rQFC) require the existence of a classical background metric. In perturbative quantum gravity, one starts with a classical background gi​jg_{ij} and quantizes graviton fluctuations δ​g^i​j\delta\hat{g}_{ij} (along with any matter fields) on that background. Therefore, backreaction is described by a δ​g^i​j\delta\hat{g}_{ij} operator in general, not a classical field. In particular, the fluctuations, i.e., ⟨δ​g^i​j2⟩−⟨δ​g^i​j⟩2\langle\delta\hat{g}_{ij}^{2}\rangle-\langle\delta\hat{g}_{ij}\rangle^{2}, may be large, and therefore it is only at the zeroth order in GG expansion where we get to describe the geometry classically.

The need for a classical background to use our definition of Θ\Theta then forces us to consider only the leading in GG term in the generalized entropy functional (1.1), namely, the A⁡(ð​𝒲)/4​GA(\eth\mathcal{W})/4G term. In particular, it would be inconsistent to include, say a correction to SgenS_{\rm gen} such as the renormalized entropy term without also including an analogous GG correction to the metric which, as discussed, is described by an operator.1818 18 Another way to see why we cannot include say the renormalized entropy corrections to the generalized entropy of a general wedge is the absence of a satisfactory prescription for computing the von Neuman entropy of gravitons in an arbitrary wedge. This is an issue since, in perturbative quantum gravity, the graviton entropy can be of the same order as the matter entropy in general. Forgoing the renormalized entropy contribution to SgenS_{\rm gen} would be a tremendous limitation because many non-trivial applications of semiclassical constraints like the rQFC are hidden in the renormalized entropy contribution (e.g., the generalized second law: Θ≥0\Theta\geq 0 on the horizon of an evaporating black hole due to Hawking radiation). At the same time, defining Θ\Theta including higher GG corrections would require extending the definition (1.2) to incorporate notions of the wedge and the null direction in a (perturbatively) quantum geometry. While this is an interesting technical challenge, here we resort to a simpler way to get around this issue. It is feasible that our results can be extended without much modification to the perturbative quantum gravity regime once the quantum geometry hurdle is overcome.1919 19 For instance, in [71], the generalized second law for perturbations to a Killing horizon was proved in perturbative quantum gravity. A crucial step was to define the area of cuts of the horizon as an operator.

In order to have a classical geometry on which the generalized entropy functional includes correction including the renormalized entropy term, a standard approach is to consider a semiclassical gravity regime involving a large number cc of matter fields. The regime is defined as in Eq. (1.6) in the introduction which we reproduce here:

G→0,c​G≡ℓSd−2=fixed.\displaystyle G\to 0,~~cG\equiv\ell_{S}^{d-2}=\text{fixed}. (2.1)

Equivalently, we can view this limit as c→∞c\to\infty, with the species scale ℓS\ell_{S} held fixed. Therefore, when the matter species are excited together, we obtain ⟨Ti​j⟩∼⟨Ti​j2⟩−⟨Ti​j⟩2∼c\langle T_{ij}\rangle\sim\langle T_{ij}^{2}\rangle-\langle T_{ij}\rangle^{2}\sim c, therefore the relative fluctuations of the stress-energy tensor and in turn of the backreacted geometry go to zero in the c→∞c\to\infty limit.2020 20 To see this, let us model the total stress tensor expectation value as the sum of independent random variables x1,…,xcx_{1},\dots,x_{c} with 𝔼⁡[xa]=μ≠0\mathbb{E}[x_{a}]=\mu\neq 0 and Var⁡(xa)=σ2<∞\mathrm{Var}(x_{a})=\sigma^{2}<\infty. For the sum Sc=∑a=1cxaS_{c}=\sum_{a=1}^{c}x_{a} we have 𝔼⁡[Sc]=c​μ\mathbb{E}[S_{c}]=c\mu and Var⁡(Sc)=c​σ2\mathrm{Var}(S_{c})=c\sigma^{2}, so the relative fluctuations obey Var⁡(Sc)/𝔼[Sc]∼c−1/2\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(S_{c})}/\mathbb{E}[S_{c}]\sim c^{-1/2}.

Note that in this regime one obtains a species scale ℓS\ell_{S} which controls the backreaction of the quantum matter fields. To obtain a perturbative semiclassical gravity regime, one must set the species scale ℓS\ell_{S} much smaller than other length scales in the problem. We then expect the following effective action:

Ieffective​[gi​j]=116​π​G​∫dd​x​−g\displaystyle I_{\rm effective}[g_{ij}]=\frac{1}{16\pi G}\int d^{d}x\sqrt{-g} (R+ℓS2​(α1​R2+α2​Ri​j​Ri​j+α3​Ri​j​k​l​Ri​j​k​l)+⋯)\displaystyle\left(R+\ell_{S}^{2}\left(\alpha_{1}R^{2}+\alpha_{2}R_{ij}R^{ij}+\alpha_{3}R_{ijkl}R^{ijkl}\right)+\cdots\right)
+log⁡Zmatter​[gi​j]+⋯,\displaystyle~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~+\log Z_{\rm matter}[g_{ij}]+\cdots, (2.2)

where Ri​j​k​lR_{ijkl}, Ri​jR_{ij}, RR denote the Riemann tensor, Ricci tensor, and scalar respectively, and Zmatter​[gi​j]Z_{\rm matter}[g_{ij}] denotes the renormalized matter partition function on a spacetime with metric gi​jg_{ij}. The ellipsis on the first line denotes further higher curvature gravity terms which are suppressed by appropriate powers of ℓS\ell_{S} 2121 21 Note that are higher curvature corrections of this order are induced by the matter sector anyways, so suppressing them further would be unnatural. In general, one may include bare higher curvature terms which to enlarge the magnitude of higher curvature corrections, but since nothing in our discussion changes with such terms, the minimal ansatz of Eq. (2.2) suffices for us., and the ellipsis on the second line indicate any terms of order c​ℓSnc\ell_{S}^{n} for n>0n>0. One could also add a cosmological constant term to the action (2.2), though we have omitted it for simplicity. Also, GG and the O⁡(1)O(1) αn\alpha_{n} denote the (renormalized) Newton’s constant and Wilson coefficients respectively.2222 22 Systematically, one must start with bare couplings, matter fields action of the many fields, and a proper set of counter-terms, which then lead to renormalized parameters in the effective action (2.2).

Note that naturally, in the perturbative semiclassical regime (i.e., (2.1) with ℓS\ell_{S} perturbatively small) physical quantities organize themselves, at leading order in cc, in an all-orders expansion in ℓS\ell_{S}. This can become manifest in the action (2.2) by taking out a prefactor cc which multiplies an expansion in ℓS\ell_{S}. For example, the Einstein Hilbert term is O⁡(ℓS2−d)O(\ell_{S}^{2-d}), while the log⁡Zmatter\log Z_{\rm matter} term is O⁡(ℓS0)O(\ell_{S}^{0}) in this expansion. The generalized entropy organizes itself in a similar manner:

Sgen​(𝒲)=c⁡[A⁡(ð​𝒲)4​ℓSd−2+⋯+Sren(1)​(𝒲)+o⁡(ℓS0)],\displaystyle S_{\rm gen}(\mathcal{W})=c\left[\frac{A(\eth\mathcal{W})}{4\ell_{S}^{d-2}}+\cdots+S_{\rm ren}^{(1)}(\mathcal{W})+o(\ell_{S}^{0})\right], (2.3)

where the leading term is the usual Bekenstein-Hawking area term (recall the relation c​Gd=ℓSd−2cG_{d}=\ell_{S}^{d-2}), and Sren(1)=Sren/cS_{\rm ren}^{(1)}=S_{\rm ren}/c is the renormalized von Neumann entropy per species in 𝒲\mathcal{W}. Besides Sren(1)S_{\rm ren}^{(1)}, it is natural to lump in together all terms with non-positive powers of ℓS\ell_{S}, which we denote by Slocal​(𝒲)S_{\rm local}(\mathcal{W}). Quite generically, Slocal​(𝒲)S_{\rm local}(\mathcal{W}) is a sum of local geometric contributions:

Slocal​(𝒲)=c​∑k=0⌊d−22⌋ℐk​(ð​𝒲)ℓSd−2−2​k=A⁡(ð​𝒲)4​G+O⁡(c​ℓS4−d),\displaystyle S_{\rm local}(\mathcal{W})=c\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\frac{d-2}{2}\rfloor}\frac{\mathcal{I}_{k}(\eth\mathcal{W})}{\ell_{S}^{d-2-2k}}=\frac{A(\eth\mathcal{W})}{4G}+O(c\ell_{S}^{4-d}), (2.4)

where ℐk​(ð​𝒲)\mathcal{I}_{k}(\eth\mathcal{W}) are integrals of local (covariant) geometric data on ð​𝒲\eth{\mathcal{W}} (scalars made up of intrinsic, extrinsic, and ambient geometric tensors at ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W}). For instance, ℐ0=∫ð​𝒲dd−2​y​h\mathcal{I}_{0}=\int_{\eth\mathcal{W}}d^{d-2}y~\sqrt{h}. The higher order corrections, which are in correspondence with the higher curvature gravity corrections in the action (2.2), are known as the Dong entropy terms (see [55, 27] for a prescription to compute them).2323 23 In even dd, the last term in SlocalS_{\rm local} is independent of ℓS\ell_{S}, and it can be viewed as getting renormalized by the logarithmic divergence (present in even dd) of the regularized von Neumann entropy. See Appendix C for an explicit example of a semiclassical gravity limit in the braneworld model where the action (2.2) and SgenS_{\rm gen} expansions can be explicitly derived.

Lastly, we denote by QQ, terms in SgenS_{\rm gen} with positive powers of ℓS\ell_{S}. These contributions can be divided into local terms (which are the continuation of SlocalS_{\rm local}-type terms), and fully non-local terms. The terms QQ are not extensively discussed in the literature. In Sec. 4, we make an assumption about the order of magnitude of their contribution to ∂λΘλ\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda} which we give evidence for in Appendix C.

In the next two sections, we operate in the semiclassical gravity regime. In Sec. 3, we work with a toy model that is simple enough that the generalized entropy simply equals the “schematic form” in Eq. (1.1). However, in Sec. 4, we discuss a general CFT in d>2d>2 coupled to gravity and in the perturbative semiclassical regime. There, we follow closely the discussion of this section and work with the SgenS_{\rm gen} ansatz of Eq. (2.3). We do not believe that the employment of the semiclassical regime is the only way to make sense of the conclusion in these sections. It is merely a way to avoid the technical hurdles discussed at the beginning of this section. Generalizing the discussion beyond this limit (e.g., to the ordinary perturbative quantum gravity regime) will be left to future work.

3 The rQFC and QFC in JT gravity coupled to a QFT

In this section, we flash the basics of JT gravity (for a thorough review, see e.g., [54]). We then present the simple proof of the rQFC in JT gravity minimally coupled to a QFT. The strategy of the proof is similar to that of the proof of the quantum Bousso bound [66, 16] in JT gravity presented in [35]. In particular, we recycle a result by Almheiri, Mahajan, and Maldacena [8], rephrasing it as the rQFC. Finally, we present two JT gravity setups that exhibit explicit violations of the QFC.

JT gravity coupled to a QFT

A fruitful direction to explore quantum gravity has been to study lower dimensional toy models. The two-dimensional Einstein-Hilbert action is topological, and the associated Einstein tensor vanishes. A well-known prescription to create a non-trivial two-dimensional gravity theory is to couple the Ricci tensor to a scalar field ϕ\phi, known as the dilaton. The most general two-derivative dilaton gravity action can always be reduced to

I=116​π​G​∫d2​x​−g​(ϕ​R+U⁡(ϕ)),I=\frac{1}{16\pi G}\int d^{2}x\sqrt{-g}(\phi R+U(\phi)), (3.1)

where U⁡(ϕ)U(\phi) is the dilaton potential [54]. Our special focus, Jackiw–Teitelboim (JT) gravity, is the quantum gravity toy model obtained by adopting a linear potential U⁡(ϕ)=−Λ​ϕU(\phi)=-\Lambda\phi [45, 68], providing a solvable toy model of quantum gravity [42, 62]. When focusing on Anti-de Sitter and de Sitter space with radius of curvature L(A)​dSL_{\rm(A)dS}, we set Λ=−2/LAdS2\Lambda=-2/L_{\rm AdS}^{2} and Λ=+2/LdS2\Lambda=+2/L_{\rm dS}^{2}, respectively. The complete JT gravity action on a two-dimensional manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} reads [45, 68, 25]

IJT=116​π​G​∫ℳd2​x​−g​((ϕ0+ϕ)​R−Λ​ϕ)+18​π​G​∫∂ℳd​x​−h​(ϕ0​K+ϕ⁡(K−1)),I_{\rm JT}=\frac{1}{16\pi G}\int_{\mathcal{M}}d^{2}x\sqrt{-g}((\phi_{0}+\phi)R-\Lambda\phi)+\frac{1}{8\pi G}\int_{\partial\mathcal{M}}dx\sqrt{-h}(\phi_{0}K+\phi(K-1)), (3.2)

where we added the topological term ϕ0​R\phi_{0}R, the Gibbons-Hawking-York boundary term and the holographic counterterm “−1-1” [75, 37, 54]. In Appendix A, we review how this action can be obtained from a dimensional reduction of the dd-dimensional Einstein-Hilbert action (with d≥3d\geq 3) with cosmological constant. In this context, it is natural to define the total dilaton field:

Φ⁡(x)=ϕ0+ϕ⁡(x).\Phi(x)=\phi_{0}+\phi(x). (3.3)

The JT action (3.2) can be supplemented with matter fields coupled to the metric. We will leave this QFT sector general unless otherwise specified, but as an example we can imagine the following matter sector consisting of cc massive scalar fields:

Imatter[gi​j,ψ]=−12∑n=1c∫d2x−g(gi​j∇iψ(n)∇jψ(n)+m2ψ(n)2).\displaystyle I_{\rm matter}[g_{ij},\psi]=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{c}\int d^{2}x\sqrt{-g}~(g^{ij}\nabla_{i}\psi_{(n)}\nabla_{j}\psi_{(n)}+m^{2}\psi_{(n)}^{2}). (3.4)

As in the introduction, we are interested in the limit,

G→0,ℓS=c​G=fixed.\displaystyle G\to 0,~~\ell_{S}=cG=\text{fixed}. (3.5)

In this limit, the quantum fluctuations of the dilaton can be ignored, and one obtains the semiclassical equations of motion:

(gi​j​∇2−∇i∇j+gi​j​Λ2)​ϕ=8​π​G​⟨Ti​j⟩,\left(g_{ij}\nabla^{2}-\nabla_{i}\nabla_{j}+g_{ij}\frac{\Lambda}{2}\right)\phi=8\pi G\Braket{T_{ij}}, (3.6)

where ⟨Ti​j⟩\langle T_{ij}\rangle denotes the expectation value of the stress-energy tensor. The only difference between AdS and dS JT gravity lies in the third term on the LHS of Eq. (3.6), depending on the sign of Λ\Lambda. Of particular importance for the discussion of quantum focusing is the component of Eq. (3.6) obtained by contracting with any null vector kik^{i}:

d2​ϕd​λ2≡ki​kj​∇i​∇jϕ=−8​π​G​ki​kj​⟨Ti​j⟩≡−8​π​G​⟨Tk​k⟩,\frac{d^{2}\phi}{d{\lambda}^{2}}\equiv k^{i}k^{j}\nabla_{i}\nabla_{j}\phi=-8\pi Gk^{i}k^{j}\Braket{T_{ij}}\equiv-8\pi G\Braket{T_{kk}}, (3.7)

where we defined the derivative

dd​λ=kμ​∇μ.\frac{d}{d\lambda}=k^{\mu}\nabla_{\mu}. (3.8)

A proof of rQFC

In JT gravity coupled to matter, we associate a generalized entropy to a spacetime wedge 𝒲\mathcal{W} using the following formula:

Sgen​(𝒲)=∑iΦ⁡(Pi)4​G+Sren​(𝒲).S_{\rm gen}(\mathcal{W})=\sum_{i}\frac{\Phi(P_{i})}{4G}+S_{\rm ren}(\mathcal{W}). (3.9)

This definition is motivated by the transverse area interpretation of Φ\Phi (see Appendix A and Eq. (A.5)) and the fact that for any wedge 𝒲\mathcal{W} in d=2d=2, we have:

ð​𝒲=⋃iPi,\displaystyle\eth\mathcal{W}=\bigcup_{i}P_{i}, (3.10)

where {Pi}\{P_{i}\} is a discrete set of points. See Fig. 3 for a schematic picture of the setup.

The QFT entropy term Sren​(𝒲)S_{\rm ren}(\mathcal{W}) contains a universal logarithmic divergence, which is irrelevant for our purposes since we are only interested in differences of SgenS_{\rm gen} between wedges.

Let us comment on the origin of Eq. (3.9) from the d=2d=2 perspective. It is a cutoff-independent quantity, well defined in the perturbative regime, which is a non-trivial property that must be satisfied by the von Neumann entropy of subregions in semiclassical gravity and JT gravity [74, 57]. Moreover, the QFC which we are about to define is directly related to fundamental constraints on the algebraic structure of the theory, which yields a definition of entropy consistent with euclidean computations [57]. Finally, the generalized entropy (3.9) was shown to be identical to the Wald entropy, which is the Noether charge associated with a bifurcation point of a Killing horizon [56].2424 24 In two dimensions, any point of dS or AdS is the bifurcation point of a Killing horizon, so that a Wald entropy can be associated with any point. Additionally, the authors of [56] discussed the thermodynamics of generalized entropy, deriving a generalized first and second law.

Following Eq. (1.2), the quantum expansion at a given point in ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} is given by:

Θλ=4​GΦ​d​Sgend​λ,\Theta_{\lambda}=\frac{4G}{\Phi}\frac{dS_{\rm gen}}{d\lambda}, (3.11)

where Sgen=Sgen​(𝒲λ)S_{\rm gen}=S_{\rm gen}(\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}), with 𝒲λ\mathcal{W}_{\lambda} a 11-parameter family of wedges parametrized by the affine parameter on the lightray emanating from one of the points in ð​𝒲λ\eth\mathcal{W_{\lambda}} (See Fig. 3). The division by Φ\Phi accounts for the factor h\sqrt{h} in Eq. (1.2), given the transverse area interpretation of Φ\Phi in this model. In the classical limit, the quantum expansion Θλ\Theta_{\lambda} reduces to the classical expansion θλ\theta_{\lambda}:

Θλ→ℏ→0θλ=1Φ​d​Φd​λ.\Theta_{\lambda}\xrightarrow[\hbar\rightarrow 0]{}\theta_{\lambda}=\frac{1}{\Phi}\frac{d\Phi}{d\lambda}. (3.12)

This quantity has no direct interpretation in JT gravity seen as a genuine two-dimensional theory. However, it can be seen as the dimensional reduction of the expansion scalar in higher dimension. In particular, we review in Appendix A that it satisfies the classical focusing theorem under the null energy condition.

In this section, the only variable of interest will be λ\lambda. We will thus make the dependence on this variable implicit: Θλ=Θ\Theta_{\lambda}=\Theta, θλ=θ\theta_{\lambda}=\theta, and write d/dλ=′d/d\lambda=~^{\prime}.

Next, to make contact with quantum focusing, we take an additional derivative of Eq. (3.11) with respect to λ\lambda, obtaining:

Θ′=−8​π​G​⟨Tk​k⟩Φ−θ2+4​G​(Sren′′Φ−θ​Sren′Φ),\Theta^{\prime}=-8\pi G\frac{\Braket{T_{kk}}}{\Phi}-\theta^{2}+4G\left(\frac{S_{\rm ren}^{\prime\prime}}{\Phi}-\frac{\theta S_{\rm ren}^{\prime}}{\Phi}\right), (3.13)

where we used the equations of motion (3.7). The quantum null energy condition (QNEC) in two dimensions reads [16]:

2​π​⟨Tk​k⟩≥Sren′′,2\pi\Braket{T_{kk}}\geq S_{\rm ren}^{\prime\prime}, (3.14)

and was proven in two-dimensional holographic QFT and CFT [48, 8].

Combined with (3.13), and assuming Φ>0\Phi>0,2525 25 In the regions where Φ<0\Phi<0, one gets Θ′≥−θ​Θ\Theta^{\prime}\geq-\theta\Theta. While solutions with Φ<0\Phi<0 are admissible when JT gravity is treated as a genuine two-dimensional theory, they are excluded if JT arises from dimensional reduction, where Φ>0\Phi>0 by construction. An additional motivation to take Φ>0\Phi>0 is that G/ΦG/\Phi may be interpreted as an effective coupling constant. We therefore find the restriction to Φ>0\Phi>0 natural on physical grounds. the QNEC (3.14) provides an upper bound on Θ′\Theta^{\prime}:

Θ′≤−θ​Θ.\Theta^{\prime}\leq-\theta\Theta. (3.15)

This inequality implies the restricted quantum focusing conjecture: for Θ=0\Theta=0, one gets Θ′≤0\Theta^{\prime}\leq 0.

It is not clear whether this statement directly maps to higher dimensions. In particular, our derivation of this upper bound relies on the two-dimensional QNEC. This energy bound is not universally valid in semiclassical gravity. In particular, in d>2d>2 spacetime dimensions, it only applies to null hypersurface with vanishing expansion [15], as explained in the introduction. We therefore do not expect the bound Θ′≤−θ​Θ\Theta^{\prime}\leq-\theta\Theta to be related to an exact statement in semiclassical gravity in d>2d>2 dimensions.

Necessary condition for QFC violations

The lower bound (3.15) provides a necessary condition for violations of the QFC in the physical spacetime regions where Φ>0\Phi>0:

Θ′>0⟹θ​Θ<0.\Theta^{\prime}>0\implies\theta\Theta<0. (3.16)

Although this condition is not sufficient, it is restrictive enough to hint at where to look if one wants to find a violation of the QFC. The condition (3.16) implies that a surface violating the QFC should lie on a lightsheet that is not a quantum lightsheet, or vice versa.2626 26 A lighsheet is a codimension-11 null hypersurface with θ≤0\theta\leq 0. A quantum lighsheet is a codimension-11 null hypersurface with Θ≤0\Theta\leq 0. This type of null hypersurface exists in backgrounds with strong quantum effects, such as an evaporating horizon.

In particular, for conformal matter, we expect violations to appear in regimes where ℓS≳ϕ0\ell_{S}\gtrsim\phi_{0} and ℓS≳ϕr\ell_{S}\gtrsim\phi_{r}. In a two-dimensional CFT, the QNEC (3.14) implies the stronger inequality 2​π​⟨Tk​k⟩−Sren′′−6c​(Sren′)2≥02\pi\Braket{T_{kk}}-S_{\rm ren}^{\prime\prime}-\frac{6}{c}(S_{\rm ren}^{\prime})^{2}\geq 0 [72]. Inserting this into Θ′\Theta^{\prime} leads to:

Θ′​Φ2\displaystyle\Theta^{\prime}\Phi^{2} ≤−(Φ′+2​ℓSc​Sren′)2−24​ℓSc2​(Sren′)2​(Φ−ℓS6).\displaystyle\leq-\left(\Phi^{\prime}+\frac{2\ell_{S}}{c}S_{\rm ren}^{\prime}\right)^{2}-\frac{24\ell_{S}}{c^{2}}(S_{\rm ren}^{\prime})^{2}\left(\Phi-\frac{\ell_{S}}{6}\right). (3.17)

QFC violations thus necessitate Φ<ℓS/6\Phi<\ell_{S}/6. Consider a conformal vacuum state taking the large cc limit. Then,

Φ⁡(x)=ϕ0+ϕr​ℱ​(x)+ℓS​𝒢​(x),\Phi(x)=\phi_{0}+\phi_{r}\mathcal{F}(x)+\ell_{S}\mathcal{G}(x), (3.18)

where ϕr​ℱ​(x)\phi_{r}\mathcal{F}(x) is the solution to the classical equations of motion without matter, and 𝒢⁡(x)\mathcal{G}(x) is the state-dependent contribution to Φ\Phi. Inserting (3.18) into (3.17), we find

Θ′|ℓSϕ0,ℓSϕr→0≤0.\Theta^{\prime}|_{\frac{\ell_{S}}{\phi_{0}},\frac{\ell_{S}}{\phi_{r}}\rightarrow 0}\leq 0. (3.19)

QFC violations can thus appear only when treating JT gravity coupled to matter as a genuine two-dimensional theory (still imposing G→0G\rightarrow 0, c→∞c\rightarrow\infty at ℓS=c​G\ell_{S}=cG fixed to ensure the semiclassical limit), allowing quantum matter effects to be large. On the other hand, Eq. (3.19) guarantees the validity of the QFC in regimes where semiclassical JT gravity has a higher-dimensional interpretation:

ϕ0≫ϕr≫ℓS,\phi_{0}\gg\phi_{r}\gg\ell_{S}, (3.20)

which requires matter quantum contributions to be small compared to classical terms (ϕr≫ℓS\phi_{r}\gg\ell_{S}), and that the dynamical dilaton field corresponds to a perturbation around an extremal black hole (ϕ0≫ϕr\phi_{0}\gg\phi_{r}). See Appendix A.2727 27 Note that while ϕ0≫ϕr\phi_{0}\gg\phi_{r} is enough to treat the gravitational part of the action as a spherical reduction of Einstein gravity, the two-dimensional matter content is not derived from a higher-dimensional model, such that semiclassical JT gravity cannot be treated as dimensional reduction of semiclassical gravity in the strictest sense.

In the remainder of this section, we present two examples of semiclassical JT gravity setups that violate the QFC. We use units where L(A)​dS=1L_{\rm(A)dS}=1.

AdS2 black hole in equilibrium with a bath

Following [7, 8], we first consider an extremal black hole in AdS2, in equilibrium with a bath modeling the asymptotically flat region far away from the black hole where gravity can be neglected. The two pieces of this toy model are constructed in semiclassical JT gravity, with one half of two-dimensional Minkowski space glued to the Poincaré patch of an extremal AdS2 black hole along its conformal boundary, see Fig. 4.

The Minkowski half-space is described in null coordinates (u,v)(u,v) with v>uv>u, while the black hole side is described by Poincaré coordinates (U,V)(U,V) where U>VU>V, with metric:

d​s2=−4​d​U​d​V(U−V)2.ds^{2}=-\frac{4dUdV}{(U-V)^{2}}. (3.21)

We consider the black hole to be in the Poincaré vacuum TU​V=TU​U=TV​V=0T_{UV}=T_{UU}=T_{VV}=0 [65]. The bath is taken to be at zero temperature as it is in equilibrium with the extremal black hole, such that Tu​v=Tu​u=Tv​v=0T_{uv}=T_{uu}=T_{vv}=0. Transparent boundary conditions imply that (u,v)=(U,V)(u,v)=(U,V) with a unique vanishing stress-energy tensor [8]. The solution to the dilaton equations of motion (3.7) in the gravity region U>VU>V is:

Φ=ϕ0+2​ϕrU−V.\Phi=\phi_{0}+\frac{2\phi_{r}}{U-V}. (3.22)

In (3.9), we approximated the gravitational part of the entropy to be given by the area term. To ensure its validity, we impose U−V≪ϕrU-V\ll\phi_{r} [52]. Beyond this regime, the gravitation theory becomes strongly coupled with a divergent effective gravitational constant (G/ΦG/\Phi), and the bulk does not have a simple description. The entanglement entropy of a wedge 𝒲\mathcal{W}, whose edge ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} is the union of a point P=(U,V)P=(U,V) in AdS and a point A=(UA,VA)A=(U_{A},V_{A}) in the Minkowski bath, is given by:

Sren​(𝒲)=c12​log⁡[(U−UA)2​(V−VA)2(U−V)2]+constant.S_{\rm ren}(\mathcal{W})=\frac{c}{12}\log\left[\frac{(U-U_{A})^{2}(V-V_{A})^{2}}{(U-V)^{2}}\right]+{\rm constant}. (3.23)

The term (U−V)2(U-V)^{2} in the denominator comes from the warp factor of the AdS2 metric at the point PP, and the constant term contains the bath UV cutoff. From now on, we fix AA at the origin, (UA,VA)=(0,0)(U_{A},V_{A})=(0,0), and let PP free in the AdS region spacelike separated to AA, i.e. in the region U>0U>0, V<0V<0. We denote by θ\theta and Θ\Theta the classical and quantum expansions associated with such point PP, respectively.

As described in Eq. (3.16), spacetime regions where violations of the QFC might happen can be probed by investigating the sign of the quantity θ​Θ\theta\Theta. Let us consider a light-ray at fixed UU, along the null direction VV, in the AdS region U>VU>V . Its classical expansion θ=Φ′/Φ\theta=\Phi^{\prime}/\Phi satisfies θ>0\theta>0, as can be seen from Eq. (3.22). If U<3​ϕr/ℓSU<3\phi_{r}/\ell_{S}, then Θ>0\Theta>0 for

V<−U23​ϕrℓS−U,V<-\frac{U^{2}}{\frac{3\phi_{r}}{\ell_{S}}-U}, (3.24)

and Θ<0\Theta<0 otherwise. If U>3​ϕr/ℓSU>3\phi_{r}/\ell_{S}, then Θ<0\Theta<0 for any V<0V<0 . The region where θ​Θ<0\theta\Theta<0 is shown in dark red in Fig. 4.

In the limit ϕr≫ℓS\phi_{r}\gg\ell_{S}, it shrinks to a narrow strip along the future horizon and the null line V=0V=0.

We find QFC violations in the region θ​Θ<0\theta\Theta<0, for a large range of parameters satisfying ℓS≳max⁡(ϕ0,ϕr)\ell_{S}\gtrsim{\rm max}(\phi_{0},\phi_{r}) , without restriction on the ratio ϕ0/ϕr\phi_{0}/\phi_{r}. We provide a schematic picture of the violation region in purple in Fig. 4, and plot the function Θ′\Theta^{\prime} along the null direction −V-V at fixed U=1U=1 in Fig. 5.

The analysis for the classical and quantum expansion is analogous for lightrays along UU, as the expressions (3.22) and (3.23) are symmetric around U=−VU=-V.

One can also consider a black hole at finite temperature. In this case, we find that QFC violations require a specific choice of Polyakov cosmological constant in the JT gravity action.2828 28 When considering ImatterI_{\rm matter} to be a classical CFT, semiclassical backreaction is described by the Polyakov action [59] which in general includes a cosmological constant term proportional to λ​Λ\lambda\Lambda, where λ\lambda is a parameter [32]. We find QFC violations for an unconventional gauge choice λ=1\lambda=1, which eliminates semiclassical corrections to the dilaton.

Evaporating de Sitter horizon

Our second example of QFC violation is obtained by considering an evaporating de Sitter cosmological horizon, modeled in semiclassical JT gravity with positive cosmological constant. We are interested in the so-called full reduction model, characterized by a non-vanishing topological term ϕ0>0\phi_{0}>0 as written in the action (3.2). The geometry contains both a black hole and cosmological horizon, surrounding the static patch of a freely falling observer (see e.g.[67] for a review of the full reduction model of de Sitter JT gravity).

The Kruskal coordinates (x+,x−)(x^{+},x^{-}) cover the static patches of two antipodal observers together with the expanding region of the de Sitter geometry behind their cosmological horizons. The metric in Kruskal coordinates is given by:

d​s2=−4(1−x+​x−)2​d​x+​d​x−.ds^{2}=-\frac{4}{(1-x^{+}x^{-})^{2}}dx^{+}dx^{-}. (3.25)

Another relevant set of coordinates are the static null coordinates (σ+,σ−)(\sigma^{+},\sigma^{-}) covering the static patch associated with the south pole observer and related to the Kruskal coordinates by x±=±e±σ±x^{\pm}=\pm e^{\pm\sigma^{\pm}}. The metric in null static coordinates is given by:

d​s2=−1cosh2⁡(σ+−σ−2)​d​σ+​d​σ−.ds^{2}=-\frac{1}{\cosh^{2}\left(\frac{\sigma^{+}-\sigma^{-}}{2}\right)}d\sigma^{+}d\sigma^{-}. (3.26)

The most common choice of vacuum state for the conformal matter is the Bunch-Davies state [21], obtained when the static patch is in thermal equilibrium with the exterior region, namely when there is equal ingoing and outgoing radiation in the static patch. It is analogous to the Minkowski vacuum [36, 26, 69] in flat space or the Hartle-Hawking state [41] of a black hole in thermal equilibrium with its Hawking radiation. In the Bunch-Davies vacuum, T±⁣±(x)​(x±)=0T_{\pm\pm}^{(x)}(x^{\pm})=0, while T±⁣±(x)​(σ±)=c/(48​π)T_{\pm\pm}^{(x)}(\sigma^{\pm})=c/(48\pi). This vacuum state is seen from a static observer as a thermal state at temperature β−1=1/2​π\beta^{-1}=1/2\pi. Another vacuum of interest is the static vacuum, which characterizes the state of a static observer in the σ±\sigma^{\pm} coordinates. It is analogous to the Rindler vacuum in flat space or the Boulware vacuum of a black hole [14, 65], and obtained by considering T±⁣±(σ)​(σ±)=0T_{\pm\pm}^{(\sigma)}(\sigma^{\pm})=0, while T±⁣±(σ)(x±)=−c/(48π(x±)2)T_{\pm\pm}^{(\sigma)}(x^{\pm})=-c/(48\pi(x^{\pm})^{2}). This state is seen as empty by a static observer following the trajectory σ+=σ−\sigma^{+}=\sigma^{-}.

Inspired by evaporating black holes, a vacuum state describing the evaporation of the de Sitter cosmological horizon can also be considered, in analogy with the Unruh vacuum of a black hole: the so-called Unruh-de Sitter state [1, 65, 69]. Such evaporation occurs when there is a positive net incoming energy flux on the static patch. Therefore, the Unruh-de Sitter state is obtained by considering asymmetrical vacuum states for the left and right-moving modes. The easiest possibility is to build a hybrid state of the Bunch-Davies and static de Sitter vacua, for the incoming and outgoing modes respectively. Considering the static patch with x+​x−≤0x^{+}x^{-}\leq 0, such state is thus defined by:

T+⁣+(σ)​(x+)\displaystyle T_{++}^{(\sigma)}(x^{+}) =−c48​π​(x+)2,\displaystyle=-\frac{c}{48\pi(x^{+})^{2}}, T+⁣+(σ)​(σ+)\displaystyle T_{++}^{(\sigma)}(\sigma^{+}) =0,\displaystyle=0, (3.27)
T−⁣−(x)​(x−)\displaystyle T_{--}^{(x)}(x^{-}) =0,\displaystyle=0, T−⁣−(x)​(σ−)\displaystyle T_{--}^{(x)}(\sigma^{-}) =c48​π.\displaystyle=\frac{c}{48\pi}. (3.28)

The equations of motion of the dilaton (3.6) are then solved by

ΦUdS​(x+,x−)=ϕ0+ϕr​1+x+​x−1−x+​x−+ℓS6​(1−1+x+​x−1−x+​x−​log⁡x+),\Phi_{\rm UdS}(x^{+},x^{-})=\phi_{0}+\phi_{r}\frac{1+x^{+}x^{-}}{1-x^{+}x^{-}}+\frac{\ell_{S}}{6}\left(1-\frac{1+x^{+}x^{-}}{1-x^{+}x^{-}}\log x^{+}\right), (3.29)

with x+>0x^{+}>0. The dilaton is therefore divergent on the past cosmological horizon x+=0x^{+}=0 of an observer at the south pole, and on its future black hole horizon x+=+∞x^{+}=+\infty. It diverges to +∞+\infty and −∞-\infty at future infinity for x<x0+x<x_{0}^{+} or x>x0+x>x_{0}^{+} respectively, where x0+≡e6​ϕr/ℓSx_{0}^{+}\equiv e^{6\phi_{r}/\ell_{S}}. The Penrose diagram of the backreacted geometry is shown in Fig. 6.

The sign of the backreacted classical expansion θ\theta of a given light-ray in the x+x^{+} direction can be easily obtained by computing ∂+ΦUdS\partial_{+}\Phi_{\rm UdS}. One finds that ∂+ΦUdS≤0\partial_{+}\Phi_{\rm UdS}\leq 0 for δ−​(x+)<x−<δ+​(x+)\delta_{-}(x^{+})<x^{-}<\delta_{+}(x^{+}), where δ±​(x+)\delta_{\pm}(x^{+}) are the curves parameterized by:

δ±​(x+)=1x+​(log⁡x+x0+±1+(log⁡x+x0+)2).\delta_{\pm}(x^{+})=\frac{1}{x^{+}}\left(\log\frac{x^{+}}{x_{0}^{+}}\pm\sqrt{1+\left(\log\frac{x^{+}}{x_{0}^{+}}\right)^{2}}\right). (3.30)

The entanglement entropy of a wedge 𝒲\mathcal{W}, whose edge is defined as the union of P=(x+,x−)P=(x^{+},x^{-}) and B=(xB+,xB−)B=(x_{B}^{+},x_{B}^{-}), is given by [2]:

Sren​(𝒲)=c12​log⁡[x+​xB+​(x−−xB−)2​[log⁡(xB+/x+)]2(1−x+​x−)2​(1−xB+​xB−)2]+constant.S_{\rm ren}(\mathcal{W})=\frac{c}{12}\log\left[\frac{x^{+}x_{B}^{+}~(x^{-}-x_{B}^{-})^{2}~[\log(x_B^+/x^+)]^{2}}{(1-x^{+}x^{-})^{2}(1-x_{B}^{+}x_{B}^{-})^{2}}\right]+{\rm constant}. (3.31)

BB is arbitrary and will be sent to spatial infinity at the end of the computation, see Fig. 6. The sign of the quantum expansion Θ\Theta of a light-ray in the x+x^{+} direction is obtained by computing ∂+Sgen\partial_{+}S_{\rm gen}. After sending xB±→±∞x_{B}^{\pm}\rightarrow\pm\infty, one finds that ∂+Sgen≥0\partial_{+}S_{\rm gen}\geq 0 for η−​(x+)<x−<η+​(x+)\eta_{-}(x^{+})<x^{-}<\eta_{+}(x^{+}), where η±​(x+)\eta_{\pm}(x^{+}) are the curves parameterized by:

η±​(x+)=1x+​(−log⁡x+x0+±1+(log⁡x+x0+)2).\eta_{\pm}(x^{+})=\frac{1}{x^{+}}\left(-\log\frac{x^{+}}{x_{0}^{+}}\pm\sqrt{1+\left(\log\frac{x^{+}}{x_{0}^{+}}\right)^{2}}\right). (3.32)

The curves δ±\delta_{\pm} and η−\eta_{-} are drawn on the Penrose diagram of Fig. 6, while the curve η+\eta_{+} lies in the region where ΦUdS<0\Phi_{\rm UdS}<0, depicted in gray. The regions where θ​Θ<0\theta\Theta<0 along x+x^{+} are shaded in red. They correspond to the regions where violations of the QFC along x+x^{+} can occur. In the limit ϕr≫ℓS\phi_{r}\gg\ell_{S}, x0+x_{0}^{+} goes to +∞+\infty while the curves δ+\delta_{+} and η−\eta_{-} get closer to the cosmological horizons x±=0x^{\pm}=0. In this regime, the regions where violations of the QFC could occur therefore consist of narrow strips along the horizons.

In the regime ℓS≳max⁡(ϕ0,ϕr)\ell_{S}\gtrsim{\rm max}(\phi_{0},\phi_{r}), independently of the ratio ϕ0/ϕr\phi_{0}/\phi_{r}, violations of the QFC along x+x^{+} are found. We schematically depict the violation region in this regime in purple in Fig. 6, and plot the functions Θ′\Theta^{\prime} and ΦUdS\Phi_{\rm UdS} along the null direction x+x^{+} at fixed x−=0.5x^{-}=0.5 in Fig. 7.

In order to maintain contact with the higher-dimensional origin of JT gravity, the region where ΦUdS<0\Phi_{\rm UdS}<0 is not considered physical and should be removed from the spacetime. However, QFC violations occur even in the physical region where ΦUdS>0\Phi_{\rm UdS}>0.

4 New 𝒅>𝟐d>2 CFT bound from the rQFC

In this section, we test the rQFC in a particular setting in d>2d>2 perturbative semiclassical gravity regime. We discover that the rQFC implies a novel stronger-than-QNEC bound in all CFTs.2929 29 The reader may wonder why instead of all CFTs, we do not demand the new constraint only of CFTs which arise as low energy limits of consistent UV-complete theories of quantum gravity. Historically, similar gravitational constraints, like the generalized second law (GSL), end up implying things about the low energy QFT sector (monotonicity of relative entropy in the case of the GSL) which are true in general QFT [71]. So demanding the validity of the new constraint in all CFTs is informed by this precedent. To obtain this result, we make crucial use of [9] which relates von Neumann entropy of null deformed Rindler wedges to light-ray operators. We end by speculating about a more universal strengthened QNEC.

Consider cc identical CFTs in the Minkowski vacuum in d>2d>2, and let 𝒲\mathcal{W}, be the domain of dependence of a spatial ball with radius RR. Let us work with the following coordinates in a neighborhood of ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} (which is located at u=v=0u=v=0):

d​s2=−d​u​d​v+R2​(1+v−u2​R)2​d​Ωd−22,\displaystyle ds^{2}=-du\,dv+R^{2}\left(1+\frac{v-u}{2R}\right)^{2}d\Omega_{d-2}^{2}, (4.1)

where d​Ωd−22d\Omega_{d-2}^{2} is the metric of a unit (d−2)(d-2)-sphere. Below, we will refer to these transverse coordinates collectively as yay^{a}, but also often single out an angle 0≤χ≤π0\leq\chi\leq\pi among them with the following:

d​Ωd−22=d​χ2+sin2​χ​d​Ωd−32.\displaystyle d\Omega_{d-2}^{2}=d\chi^{2}+\sin^{2}\chi~d\Omega_{d-3}^{2}. (4.2)

By translating ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} along ∂+𝒲\partial^{+}\mathcal{W} by an affine length v=V⁡(ya)v=V(y^{a}) we can obtain another wedge. Let us pick the following one-parameter family of such wedges labeled by λ\lambda:

Vλ​(ya)=λ​exp⁡(11−Σ2/R2​χ2),|χ|≤ΣR,\displaystyle V_{\lambda}(y^{a})=\lambda\exp\left(\frac{1}{1-\Sigma^{2}/R^{2}\chi^{2}}\right),~~|\chi|\leq\frac{\Sigma}{R}, (4.3)

and Vλ​(ya)=0V_{\lambda}(y^{a})=0 elsewhere. Therefore, the parameter Σ\Sigma determines the characteristic transverse width of the deformation profile (see left Fig. 8). As we will see later in the section, dialing this width appropriately small will expose new implications of rQFC.

We take the perturbative semiclassical limit by sending c→∞c\to\infty (or equivalently G→0G\to 0), while holding the species scale ℓS=(c​G)1/d−2\ell_{S}=(cG)^{1/d-2} fixed. We further take ℓS\ell_{S} to be perturbatively small compared to the physical scales of the problem (e.g., the size of the ball and the scale associated with the state). For a non-trivial test of rQFC, let us consider a “near-vacuum” state |Ψ⟩\ket{\Psi} by acting on the vacuum with a unitary operator:

|Ψ⟩=exp⁡(i​ϵ​∑q=1cOf(q))​|0⟩,\displaystyle\ket{\Psi}=\exp(i \epsilon\sum_{q=1}^c O^{(q)}_f)\ket{0}, (4.4)

where ϵ≪1\epsilon\ll 1 and Of(q)O^{(q)}_{f} denotes a Hermitian operator in sector qq smeared by some compact smearing function ff (taken to be a scalar for simplicity). Explicitly,

Of(q)=∫dd​x​f​(x)​O(q)​(x).\displaystyle O^{(q)}_{f}=\int d^{d}x~f(x)O^{(q)}(x). (4.5)

To keep the analysis simpler, we will choose Of(q)O^{(q)}_{f} such that the entropy derivatives change non-trivially (see Eq. (2.3)), but the geometry in a neighborhood of the null deformation (Eq. (4.3)) remains unchanged. This can happen if the support of OO stays away from this region. For example, we can pick:

Of(q)=Φf1(q)​Φf2(q),\displaystyle O^{(q)}_{f}=\Phi^{(q)}_{f_{1}}\Phi^{(q)}_{f_{2}}, (4.6)

where smearing functions f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} are chosen to have compact support on a ball-shaped spacetime region with radius L≪RL\ll R, and is placed a spatial distance LL on the left and right side of ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} around the locus of null deformation (see Fig. 9). Since this operator is unitary and is placed at spacelike separation to the locus of deformation, it does not inject any energy there. Note that this operator needs to be properly gravitationally dressed to be well-defined. But we are free to choose a dressing which does not change the geometry in a neighborhood of the null deformation, so to all orders in the ℓS\ell_{S} perturbation theory the geometry is flat and:

θλ​(χ=0)=d−22​R,\displaystyle\theta_{\lambda}(\chi=0)=\frac{d-2}{2R}, (4.7)

where θλ\theta_{\lambda} is the expansion of the congruence (4.3).

Recall from Sec.2, that in the perturbative semiclassical regime the generalized entropy can be written as an expansion in ℓS\ell_{S}:

Sgen​(𝒲)=c⁡[A⁡(ð​𝒲)4​ℓSd−2+⋯+Sren(1)​(𝒲)+Q],\displaystyle S_{\rm gen}(\mathcal{W})=c\left[\frac{A(\eth\mathcal{W})}{4\ell_{S}^{d-2}}+\cdots+S_{\rm ren}^{(1)}(\mathcal{W})+Q\right], (4.8)

where Sren(1)=Sren/cS^{(1)}_{\rm ren}=S_{\rm ren}/c, is the renormalized entropy per species, and all the terms before SrenS_{\rm ren} are the geometrically local terms resulting from higher curvature corrections to Einstein gravity (see Eq. (2.4)).3030 30 Recall that such higher curvature corrections will be induced in the semiclassical limit anyways, so it would be unnatural to ignore them, though we will show that they are inconsequential for the argument. They only depend on the local geometry of ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} (intrinsic and extrinsic geometry of ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W}, and also the ambient Ri​j​k​lR_{ijkl} there) and the ambient local geometry. Lastly, the term QQ denotes all contributions of o⁡(ℓS0)o(\ell_{S}^{0}).

We can obtain an explicit expression for Θλ\Theta_{\lambda} from Eq. (4.8) (see the definition in Eq. (1.2)):

Θλ(ya)=θλ(ya)+⋯+4​ℓSd−2hλδ​Sren(1)δ​V​(ya)|λ+o(ℓSd−2),\displaystyle\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=\theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})+\cdots+\frac{4\ell_{S}^{d-2}}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\left.\frac{\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}+o(\ell_{S}^{d-2}), (4.9)

where ellipsis denote contributions from SlocalS_{\rm local}, which are therefore suppressed at leading by a factor of ℓS2/R\ell_{S}^{2}/R. Therefore, the rQFC condition Θλ​(ya)=0\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=0 implies:

θλ(ya)=−4​ℓSd−2hλδ​Sren(1)δ​V​(ya)|λ+o(ℓSd−2),\displaystyle\theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=-\frac{4\ell_{S}^{d-2}}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}^{(1)}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}+o(\ell_{S}^{d-2}), (4.10)

because this equation in particular implies R∼ℓS2−dR\sim\ell_{S}^{2-d}, which when plugged into Eq. (4.9) makes the ellipsis terms subleading to the renormalized entropy terms.

We can also compute ∂λΘλ\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}:

∂λΘλ=−θλ2d−2+⋯−4​ℓSd−2​θλhλδ​Sren(1)δ​V​(ya)|λ+4​ℓSd−2h∂λδ​Sren(1)δ​V​(ya)|λ+o(ℓSd−2),\displaystyle\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}=-\frac{\theta_{\lambda}^{2}}{d-2}+\cdots-\frac{4\ell_{S}^{d-2}\theta_{\lambda}}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}^{(1)}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}+\frac{4\ell_{S}^{d-2}}{\sqrt{h}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}^{(1)}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}+o(\ell_{S}^{d-2}), (4.11)

where we have used the flatness of the ambient geometry in a neighborhood of the deformation to set the shear-squared ς2=0\varsigma^{2}=0, and Ri​j=0R_{ij}=0. Furthermore, the ellipsis which come from SlocalS_{\rm local} are suppressed at least by ℓS2/R2\ell_{S}^{2}/R^{2}, so R∼ℓS2−dR\sim\ell_{S}^{2-d} implies that the ellipsis terms are in particular o⁡(ℓS2​(d−2))o(\ell_{S}^{2(d-2)}).

The statement of the rQFC for the ball-shaped region is then:

Θλ​(ya)=0⟹∂λΘλ​(ya)\displaystyle\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=0\implies\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a}) =16​(d−3)d−2ℓS2​(d−2)(1hλδ​Sren(1)δ​V​(ya)|λ)2\displaystyle=\frac{16(d-3)}{d-2}\ell_{S}^{2(d-2)}\left(\left.\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\frac{\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}\right)^{2}
+4​ℓSd−2hλ∂λδ​Sren(1)δ​V​(ya)|λ+∂λ(4​ℓSd−2hλδ​Qδ​V​(ya))+o(ℓS2​(d−2))≤0.\displaystyle+\frac{4\ell_{S}^{d-2}}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}+\partial_{\lambda}\left(\frac{4\ell_{S}^{d-2}}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\frac{\delta Q}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right)+o(\ell_{S}^{2(d-2)})\leq 0. (4.12)

The o⁡(ℓS2​(d−1))o(\ell_{S}^{2(d-1)}) terms in particular consist of the contributions from the corrections in Eq. (4.10), and also of Eq. (4.11) (once we impose R∼ℓS2−dR\sim\ell_{S}^{2-d} as a consequence of Eq. (4.10)). In Appendix C, we argue that the contribution from QQ in Eq. (4.12) is also o⁡(ℓS2​(d−2))o(\ell_{S}^{2(d-2)}), that is:

∂λ(4​ℓSd−2hλ​δ​Qδ​V​(ya))=o⁡(ℓS2​(d−2)),\displaystyle\partial_{\lambda}\left(\frac{4\ell_{S}^{d-2}}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\frac{\delta Q}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right)=o(\ell_{S}^{2(d-2)}), (4.13)

which we assume from here on, and therefore we no longer explicitly write the QQ term in Eq. (4.12).

We now discuss the von Neumann entropy derivative terms (the first two terms the RHS of Eq. (4.12)). We need only to evaluate them at leading order in ℓS\ell_{S}, though higher ℓS\ell_{S} corrections can also be defined by taking into account the proper dressing of Of(q)O^{(q)}_{f}, and analyzing the backreaction. Despite the unitary (4.4) not changing the geometry near the locus of null deformation, the Of(q)O^{(q)}_{f} in Eq. (4.6) couples the inside and outside of 𝒲\mathcal{W}, and therefore can change the von Neumann entropy derivatives non-trivially. In particular, in the regime L≪RL\ll R, we expect:

1h​δ​Sren(1)δ​V​(ya)∼ϵLd−1.\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{h}}\frac{\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\sim\frac{\epsilon}{L^{d-1}}. (4.14)

Let us justify the scaling in Eq. (4.14). In the Minkowski vacuum, the only scale which could govern the LHS of Eq. (4.14) is RR. After changing the state to |Ψ⟩\ket{\Psi}, we expect that the answer can now depend non-trivially on ϵ\epsilon, LL, and RR. Suppose now that we first take RR to be very large (as required by the condition L≪RL\ll R). Then, we expect that the dependence on RR will drop out of the entropy derivative. Furthermore, in this limit, we can approximate the ball-shaped region by a Rindler wedge. Therefore, at O⁡(ϵ0)O(\epsilon^{0}) the entropy derivative must be zero.3131 31 This is simply a result of symmetry in the Rindler wedge. The transverse integral of the functional derivative in Eq. (4.14) gives the entropy shape derivative associated with moving the Rindler wedge in the null direction to an identical Rindler wedge. Therefore, the total entropy derivative must be zero. By the transverse symmetry of the Rindler wedge (in the Minkowski vacuum), the functional derivative must vanish as well. Therefore, the first non-trivial term appears at O⁡(ϵ)O(\epsilon), and the powers of LL in Eq. (4.14) is enforced by dimensional analysis. Note that it was important in this analysis that the theory is a CFT, so the only scales we need to consider are that of the region and the state. Of course the scaling dimension of the operator Of(q)O^{(q)}_{f} matters as well, but those are dimensionless and will only affect the constant of proportionality in Eq. (4.14).

Conformally transforming ∂λ(δ​Sren(1)/δ​Vλ​(ya))\partial_{\lambda}(\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}/\delta V_{\lambda}(y^{a})) into its Rindler wedge analogue

We now discuss the term ∂λ(δ​Sren(1)/δ​Vλ​(ya))\partial_{\lambda}(\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}/\delta V_{\lambda}(y^{a})) in Eq. (4.12), which is slightly more involved. In [9], this quantity was computed explicitly in an ϵ\epsilon expansion for null deformations of a Rindler wedge. We take advantage of a conformal transformation which maps 𝒲\mathcal{W} to the Rindler wedge, and its null deformations. Starting from Minkowski coordinates XiX^{i} of Eq. (4.1), we can consider a transformation to new coordinates X~i\tilde{X}^{i} using a special conformal transformation followed by a translation:

Xi=X~i−X~2​Ci1−2​(Ci​X~i)+C2​X~2+2​R2​Ci,\displaystyle X^{i}=\frac{\tilde{X}^{i}-\tilde{X}^{2}C^{i}}{1-2(C_{i}\tilde{X}^{i})+C^{2}\tilde{X}^{2}}+2R^{2}C^{i}, (4.15)

where

Ci=(X~0=0,X~1=12​R,0,⋯),\displaystyle C^{i}=\left(\tilde{X}^{0}=0,\tilde{X}^{1}=\frac{1}{2R},0,\cdots\right), (4.16)

and the inner products are with Minkowski metric ηi​j\eta_{ij}, e.g., Ci​Xi=ηi​j​Ci​XjC_{i}X^{i}=\eta_{ij}C^{i}X^{j}.3232 32 In Eq. (4.16), since χ=0\chi=0 we do not need to specify the other d−2d-2 coordinates. The relation between the metric in these coordinates is given by

Ω2​(X)​[−d​u​d​v+R2​(1+v−u2​R)2​d​Ωd−22]=−d​u~​d​v~+∑a=1d−2d​y~a2,\displaystyle\Omega^{2}(X)\left[-dudv+R^{2}\left(1+\frac{v-u}{2R}\right)^{2}d\Omega_{d-2}^{2}\right]=-d\tilde{u}d\tilde{v}+\sum_{a=1}^{d-2}d\tilde{y}_{a}^{2}, (4.17)

where

Ω⁡(X)=1−2​(Ci​Xi)+C2​X2.\displaystyle\Omega(X)=1-2(C_{i}X^{i})+C^{2}X^{2}. (4.18)

Note that in Eq. (4.17), the metric in the brackets on the LHS and RHS are both Minkowski metrics, but the coordinates are such that u=v=0u=v=0 is a (d−2)(d-2) sphere of size RR, while u~=v~=0\tilde{u}=\tilde{v}=0 is an infinite plane parametrized by polar coordinates ρ\rho and the additional (d−2)(d-2) angles. In analogy with the XiX^{i} coordinates, we refer to the transverse directions in coordinates X~i\tilde{X}^{i} collectively as y~a\tilde{y}^{a}, though as before we single out a radial coordinate ρ~\tilde{\rho} using:

∑a=1d−2d​y~a2=d​ρ~2+ρ~2​d​Ωd−32.\displaystyle\sum_{a=1}^{d-2}d\tilde{y}_{a}^{2}=d\tilde{\rho}^{2}+\tilde{\rho}^{2}d\Omega_{d-3}^{2}. (4.19)

The coordinate transformation (4.15) maps the 𝒲\mathcal{W} wedges, i.e., the domain of dependence of a ball-shaped region and its null deformations specified by v=V⁡(ya)v=V(y^{a}), into 𝒲~\tilde{\mathcal{W}}, i.e., a Rindler wedge and its corresponding null deformations specified by v~=V~​(y~a)\tilde{v}=\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a}) (see Fig. 8). Since a Weyl transformation can remove the factor of Ω2​(X)\Omega^{2}(X) in Eq. (4.17), this has implications for a CFT. In particular, it turns out that the renormalized entropy is a conformal invariant [48, 38].That is,

S~ren(1)​(V~​(y~a))=Sren(1)​(V⁡(ya)),\displaystyle\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}(\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a}))=S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}(V(y^{a})), (4.20)

where S~ren(1)​(V~​(y~a))\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}(\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})) is the renormalized entropy in the conformally transformed state of a certain deformation of a Rindler wedge, determined by V~​(y~a)\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a}). In even dimensions, there is in general an additive anomaly term in Eq. (4.20). This term will not change any of our arguments going forward, and we will absorb it in the definition of S~ren\tilde{S}_{\rm ren}.

We will restrict to V⁡(y)V(y) which only depends on χ\chi, where the map between V⁡(ya)V(y^{a}) and V~​(y~a)\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a}) simplifies. Explicitly, it is easy to derive that:

V⁡(χ)=V~​(ρ~)1+V~​(ρ~)/2​R+O⁡(ρ~2R2).\displaystyle V(\chi)=\frac{\tilde{V}(\tilde{\rho})}{1+\tilde{V}(\tilde{\rho})/2R}+O\left(\frac{\tilde{\rho}^{2}}{R^{2}}\right). (4.21)

Now, suppose we define a natural λ\lambda-parametrized family of null-deformed Rindler wedges by:

V~λ​(y~a)=λ​exp⁡(11−Σ2/ρ~2),|ρ~|≤Σ,\displaystyle\tilde{V}_{\lambda}(\tilde{y}^{a})=\lambda\exp\left(\frac{1}{1-\Sigma^{2}/\tilde{\rho}^{2}}\right),~~|\tilde{\rho}|\leq\Sigma, (4.22)

and V~λ​(y~a)=0\tilde{V}_{\lambda}(\tilde{y}^{a})=0 elsewhere. It then follows using the chain rule that:

∂λδ​S~ren(1)δ​V~λ​(y~a)|λ=∂λδ​Sren(1)δ​Vλ​(ya)|λ+1Rδ​Sren(1)δ​Vλ​(ya)|λ,\displaystyle\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}_{\lambda}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}=\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta V_{\lambda}(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}+\frac{1}{R}\left.\frac{\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta V_{\lambda}(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}, (4.23)

It is desirable to rewrite Eq. (4.23) using Eq. (4.7) as instead:

∂λδ​S~ren(1)δ​V~​(y~a)|λ=∂λδ​Sren(1)δ​V​(ya)|λ+2d−2θλδ​Sren(1)δ​V​(ya)|λ.\displaystyle\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}=\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}+\frac{2}{d-2}\theta_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}. (4.24)

Using this, we can re-write the second term in Eq. (4.12) of the other two terms in Eq. (4.24). After simplification, the statement of rQFC can be written as:

Θλ​(ya)=0⟹∂λΘλ​(ya)=16​(d−1)d−2\displaystyle\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=0\implies\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda}(y^{a})=\frac{16(d-1)}{d-2} ℓS2​(d−2)(1hλδ​Sren(1)δ​V​(ya)|λ)2\displaystyle\ell_{S}^{2(d-2)}\left(\left.\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\frac{\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}\right)^{2}
+4​ℓSd−2hλ∂λδ​S~ren(1)δ​V~​(y~a)|λ+o(ℓS2​(d−2))≤0.\displaystyle+\frac{4\ell_{S}^{d-2}}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}+o(\ell_{S}^{2(d-2)})\leq 0. (4.25)

Note that the first term on the RHS is positive, therefore the rQFC enforces that the second term must be sufficiently negative.3333 33 Note that the second term on the RHS of Eq. (4.25) is a Rindler wedge quantity in a state where ⟨Ti​j⟩​ki​kj=0\langle T_{ij}\rangle k^{i}k^{j}=0 in a neighborhood of the null deformation. Therefore, the QNEC merely implies that this term is negative (see Eq. (1.15)). However, in this setting, we see that the rQFC demands more than it being negative. It must be negative and large enough in magnitude. We discuss an explicit expression for this term next.

Explicit expression for ∂λ(δS~ren(1)/δV~(y~a))|V~λ\partial_{\lambda}(\delta\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}/\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a}))\rvert_{\tilde{V}_{\lambda}}

In [9], the LHS of Eq. (4.24) was calculated in d>2d>2.3434 34 In fact, the expression which we cite is true for any QFT, not just CFTs. We describe the setup, and present this expression from [9], and relegate a sketch of its derivation to Appendix B.

Let O~fj\tilde{O}^{j}_{f} be the result of the operator O(q)jO_{(q)}^{j} defined in Eqs. (4.5) and (4.6) after conformal transformation (4.15). We consider |Ψ⟩~\tilde{\ket{\Psi}} the near vacuum state in d>2d>2 Minkowski spacetime resulting from the conformal transformation of |Ψ⟩\ket{\Psi} defined in Eq. (4.4):

|Ψ⟩~=∑q=1cei​ϵ​O~f(q)​|0⟩,\displaystyle\tilde{\ket{\Psi}}=\sum_{q=1}^{c}e^{i\epsilon\tilde{O}^{(q)}_{f}}\ket{0}, (4.26)

where O~f=∑j=1cO~fj.\tilde{O}_{f}=\sum_{j=1}^{c}\tilde{O}^{j}_{f}.

A main result of [9] is that (see Appendix B for a review):

1h~λ∂λδ​S~ren(1)δ​V~​(y~a)|λ=0=−ϵ22∫dd−2y~′h~∂λV~λ(y~′a)∫−∞∞dses⟨O~f(1)ℰ(y~′a)ℰ(y~)O~fs(1)⟩+O(ϵ3),\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{h}_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda=0}=-\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{2}\int d^{d-2}\tilde{y}^{\prime}\sqrt{\tilde{h}}~\partial_{\lambda}\tilde{V}_{\lambda}(\tilde{y}^{\prime a})~\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}ds~e^{s}\langle\tilde{O}^{(1)}_{f}\mathcal{E}(\tilde{y}^{\prime a})\mathcal{E}(\tilde{y})\tilde{O}^{(1)}_{f_{s}}\rangle+O(\epsilon^{3}), (4.27)

where ℰ\mathcal{E} denotes the averaged null energy operator placed at transverse position y~\tilde{y}:

ℰ⁡(y~a)=∫−∞∞d​v~​Tv~​v~​(u~=0,v~,y~a),\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\tilde{y}^{a})=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\tilde{v}~T_{\tilde{v}\tilde{v}}(\tilde{u}=0,\tilde{v},\tilde{y}^{a}), (4.28)

where Tv~​v~T_{\tilde{v}\tilde{v}} denotes the indicated component of the stress-energy tensor, and O~fs(1)\tilde{O}^{(1)}_{f_{s}} is a result of evolving O~f(1)\tilde{O}^{(1)}_{f} by a global boost operator by an amount ss:

O~fs(1)=e−i​K​s​O~f(1)​ei​K​s.\displaystyle\tilde{O}^{(1)}_{f_{s}}=e^{-iKs}\tilde{O}^{(1)}_{f}e^{iKs}. (4.29)

where KK is the global boost generator. This can be arranged by boosting the profile ff to its boosted version fsf_{s}. 3535 35 For λ≠0\lambda\neq 0, Ofs(1)O^{(1)}_{f_{s}} needs to be replaced by ei​K​s​O~f(1)​e−i​K​se^{iKs}\tilde{O}^{(1)}_{f}e^{-iKs} where KK is the full modular Hamiltonian associated to the cut λ\lambda. Our conclusions are easily generalizable to arbitrary λ\lambda by this replacement.

We are interested in deriving how the LHS of Eq. (4.27) scales with the parameters involved. Specifically, let us discuss how the RHS term at O⁡(ϵ2)O(\epsilon^{2}) scales with Σ\Sigma, the transverse width of the deformation profile, and the scale LL associated to the state (as specified by the size of the smearing function in Eq. (4.27)). The dependence on Σ\Sigma is controlled by the behavior of the integrand as ℰ\mathcal{E}’s approach each other. In particular it is easy to verify that:

1h~λ∂λδ​S~ren(1)δ​V~​(y~a)|λ=0=O(ϵ2​Σd−2−δL2​d−2−δ)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{h}_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda=0}=O\left(\frac{\epsilon^{2}\Sigma^{d-2-\delta}}{L^{2d-2-\delta}}\right) (4.30)

where:

∫−∞∞d​s​es​⟨O~(1)​ℰ​(y~′a)​ℰ​(y~a)​O~fs(1)⟩=y~′→y~O⁡(|y~−y~′|−δ)\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}ds~e^{s}\langle\tilde{O}^{(1)}\mathcal{E}(\tilde{y}^{\prime a})\mathcal{E}(\tilde{y}^{a})\tilde{O}^{(1)}_{f_{s}}\rangle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{y}^{\prime}\to\tilde{y}}}{{=}}O(|\tilde{y}-\tilde{y}^{\prime}|^{{-\delta}}) (4.31)

where |y~−y~′||\tilde{y}-\tilde{y}^{\prime}| denotes proper distance between the indicated points. In Eq. (4.30), the factors of LL are put in by dimensional analysis.

We have now determined how the relevant terms in Eq. (4.25) scales with the parameters in our problem, and are in a position to extract implications of the rQFC.

Putting everything together: rQFC implies a new bound

Let us summarize the order of magnitude of the relevant terms in Eq. (4.25):

4​(d−1)d−2ℓS2​(d−2)(1hλδ​Sren(1)δ​V​(ya)|λ=0)2\displaystyle\frac{4(d-1)}{d-2}\ell_{S}^{2(d-2)}\left(\left.\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\frac{\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda=0}\right)^{2} =O⁡(ϵ2​ℓS2​(d−2)L2​(d−1))>0,\displaystyle=O\left(\epsilon^{2}\frac{\ell_{S}^{2(d-2)}}{L^{2(d-1)}}\right)>0, (4.32)
4​ℓSd−2hλ∂λδ​S~ren(1)δ​V~​(y~a)|λ=0\displaystyle\frac{4\ell_{S}^{d-2}}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda=0} =O⁡(ϵ2​ℓSd−2​Σd−2−δL2​d−2−δ)<0,\displaystyle=O\left(\epsilon^{2}\frac{\ell_{S}^{d-2}\Sigma^{d-2-\delta}}{L^{2d-2-\delta}}\right)<0, (4.33)

where in the first line the generic condition:

1hλδ​Sren(1)δ​V​(ya)|λ=0=1hλδ​S~ren(1)δ​V~​(y~a)|λ=0=O(ϵLd−1)\displaystyle\left.\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\frac{\delta S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda=0}=\left.\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\frac{\delta\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda=0}=O\left(\frac{\epsilon}{L^{d-1}}\right) (4.34)

was used. The first equality in Eq. (4.34) simply comes from the conformal transformation. And the second the inequality is the result of the QNEC, which in this particular setting, follows directly from Eq. (4.27).

For the rQFC to be valid, Eq. (4.32) must not exceed Eq. (4.33) in magnitude, since the former is positive. Furthermore, for our analysis so far to be valid, we need to remain in the semiclassical regime which requires all length scales in the problem to be much larger than ℓS\ell_{S}. In particular, we must satisfy Σ≫ℓS\Sigma\gg\ell_{S}, while also satisfying:

(ΣL)d−2−δ≳(ℓSL)d−2.\displaystyle\left(\frac{\Sigma}{L}\right)^{d-2-\delta}\gtrsim\left(\frac{\ell_{S}}{L}\right)^{d-2}. (4.35)

Therefore, the rQFC implies that δ≥0\delta\geq 0. We can summarize this bound as:

1hλδ​S~ren(1)δ​V~​(y~a)|λ=0=O(ϵLd−1)⟹1h~λ∂λδ​S~ren(1)δ​V~​(y~a)|λ=0≤O(ϵ2​Σd−2L2​d−2).\displaystyle\left.\frac{1}{\sqrt{h_{\lambda}}}\frac{\delta\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda=0}=O\left(\frac{\epsilon}{L^{d-1}}\right)\implies\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{h}_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda=0}\leq O(\frac{\epsilon^{2}\Sigma^{d-2}}{L^{2d-2}}). (4.36)

By the expression on the RHS, we mean that the second derivative of the von Neumann entropy cannot approach zero faster than Σd−2\Sigma^{d-2} as Σ→0\Sigma\to 0. This bound is stronger than the QNEC in this class of states, since the QNEC merely requires that the RHS of (4.36) is non-positive.

Let us end by suggesting a more universal bound which we speculate might be true in all QFTs and implies the above-mentioned bounds. Roughly speaking, our bound (4.36) comes from the rQFC enforcing that the QNEC does not get close to saturation as Σ→0\Sigma\to 0 by a larger power than Σd−2\Sigma^{d-2}, whenever δ​S~ren(1)/δ​V~​(y~a)≠0\delta\tilde{S}^{(1)}_{\rm ren}/\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})\neq 0 at the relevant order in ϵ\epsilon. We have made two simplifying assumptions to extract this bound. We restricted to near vacuum-states, and, in particular, to ones in which ⟨Ti​j⟩=0\langle T_{ij}\rangle=0 in a neighborhood of the deformation by picking our smearing function ff to have no support there. Certainly, one can consider states with the latter property that are not near-vacuum, e.g., by setting ϵ=1\epsilon=1 in unitaries (4.4). We then still expect some verison of the above-mentioned bound on the magnitude of (4.33) to hold. The only difference is that we cannot as directly connect it to the product of ℰ\mathcal{E} operators. Perhaps, the restriction to ⟨Ti​j⟩=0\langle T_{ij}\rangle=0 at the locus of null deformation is not essential for the argument either, and is only a convenient choice for the computation. We therefore speculate here that the following universal bound holds in the Rindler wedge for all QFTs:

2π⟨T~i​j⟩k~ik~j−1h~λ∂λδ​S~renδ​V~​(y~a)|λ≥Σ→0κΣd−2(1h~λδ​S~renδ​V~​(y~a)|λ)2,(Speculative)\displaystyle 2\pi\langle\tilde{T}_{ij}\rangle\tilde{k}^{i}\tilde{k}^{j}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{h}_{\lambda}}}\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Sigma\to 0}}{{\geq}}\kappa\Sigma^{d-2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{h}_{\lambda}}}\left.\frac{\delta\tilde{S}_{\rm ren}}{\delta\tilde{V}(\tilde{y}^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}\right)^{2},~~~~~~\text{(Speculative)} (4.37)

where κ>0\kappa>0 needs to be determined. Here, tilde denotes that everything is evaluated on the Rindler wedge, and kik^{i} denotes the (surface-orthogonal) null vector field on ∂+𝒲~\partial^{+}\tilde{\mathcal{W}} which generates the V~λ​(ya)\tilde{V}_{\lambda}(y^{a}) flow.

When applied to our near-vacuum states (4.4) in a CFT, the bound (4.37) implies Eq. (4.36). We leave further exploration of it to future work.
