Appendix A JT gravity as dimensional reduction

In addition to its solvability, one of the main reasons why JT gravity has received a lot of interest is its relation to higher-dimensional gravity. Indeed, the action (3.2) can be obtained from a dimensional reduction of the dd-dimensional Einstein-Hilbert action with cosmological constant Λ^\hat{\Lambda}:

IEH=116​π​G^​∫ℳ^dd​X​−g^​[R^−Λ^]+18​π​G^​∫∂ℳ^dd​Y​−h^​K^,I_{\rm EH}=\frac{1}{16\pi\hat{G}}\int_{\hat{\mathcal{M}}}d^{d}X\sqrt{-\hat{g}}\left[\hat{R}-\hat{\Lambda}\right]+\frac{1}{8\pi\hat{G}}\int_{\partial\hat{\mathcal{M}}}d^{d}Y\sqrt{-\hat{h}}\hat{K}, (A.1)

where G^\hat{G} is Newton’s constant on the original dd-dimensional manifold ℳ^\hat{\mathcal{M}} with coordinates {XM,M=0,…,d−1}\{X^{M},~M=0,...,d-1\}, g^M​N\hat{g}_{MN} is the metric tensor on ℳ^\hat{\mathcal{M}} and g^\hat{g} its determinant, R^\hat{R} is the Ricci scalar. {YM,M=0,…,d−2}\{Y^{M},~M=0,...,d-2\} are the coordinates on the boundary ∂ℳ^\partial\hat{\mathcal{M}} with induced metric h^M​N\hat{h}_{MN}, and K^\hat{K} is the trace of its extrinsic curvature. The radius of curvature L(A)​dSL_{\rm(A)dS} is related to the higher-dimensional cosmological constant Λ^\hat{\Lambda} by Λ^=±(d−1)(d−2)/L(A)​dS2\hat{\Lambda}=\pm(d-1)(d-2)/L_{\rm(A)dS}^{2}.

The JT gravity action (3.2) can be obtained from the metric ansatz3636 36 See, for example, Appendix A of [67] for a derivation.

d​s2=g^M​N​d​XM​d​XN=gi​j​(x)​d​xi​d​xj+L(A)​dS2​Φ2/(d−2)​(x)​d​Ωd−22.ds^{2}=\hat{g}_{MN}dX^{M}dX^{N}=g_{ij}(x)dx^{i}dx^{j}+L_{\rm(A)dS}^{2}\Phi^{2/(d-2)}(x)d\Omega_{d-2}^{2}. (A.2)

The metric gi​jg_{ij} and coordinates {xi,i=0,1}\{x^{i},~i=0,1\} describe a two-dimensional manifold ℳ\mathcal{M}, such that ℳ^=ℳ×𝕊d−1\hat{\mathcal{M}}=\mathcal{M}\crossproduct\mathbb{S}^{d-1} with the dilaton field Φ\Phi encoding the size of the (d−2)(d-2)-dimensional compact space 𝕊d−2\mathbb{S}^{d-2}. The action then reduces to

IEH=116​π​G​∫ℳd2​x​−g​[Φ​R−Λ^​Φ+(d−3)​(d−2)L(A)​dS2​Φd−4d−2+d−3d−2​(∇Φ)2Φ]+18​π​G∫∂ℳdy−hΦK,\begin{split}I_{\rm EH}=&\,\frac{1}{16\pi G}\int_{\mathcal{M}}d^{2}x\sqrt{-g}\left[\Phi R-\hat{\Lambda}\Phi+\frac{(d-3)(d-2)}{L_{\rm(A)dS}^{2}}\Phi^{\frac{d-4}{d-2}}+\frac{d-3}{d-2}\frac{(\nabla\Phi)^{2}}{\Phi}\right]\\ &+\frac{1}{8\pi G}\int_{\partial\mathcal{M}}dy\sqrt{-h}\Phi K,\end{split} (A.3)

where RR is the two-dimensional Ricci scalar, ∇\nabla the covariant derivative compatible with the metric gi​jg_{ij}, and KK the trace of the extrinsic curvature of the boundary ∂ℳ\partial\mathcal{M} of ℳ\mathcal{M}. The two-dimensional Newton constant GG is given by

1G=Sd−2​(L(A)​dS)G^,\frac{1}{G}=\frac{S_{d-2}(L_{\rm(A)dS})}{\hat{G}}, (A.4)

where Sd−2​(L(A)​dS)=2​π(d−1)/2​L(A)​dSd−2/Γ⁡((d−1)/2)S_{d-2}(L_{\rm(A)dS})=2\pi^{(d-1)/2}~L_{\rm(A)dS}^{d-2}/\Gamma((d-1)/2) is the surface area of the (d−2)(d-2)-sphere of radius L(A)​dSL_{\rm(A)dS}.

When d=3d=3, the action (A.3) simplifies to (3.2), and ϕ0=0\phi_{0}=0. It can be interpreted as the dimensional reduction of an empty (A)dS background. When spherically reducing a higher-dimensional metric with d>3d>3, the kinetic term can be removed by a Weyl rescaling gi​j→1d−1​Φ−d−3d−2​gi​jg_{ij}\rightarrow\frac{1}{d-1}\Phi^{-\frac{d-3}{d-2}}g_{ij}. One then expands around Φ=ϕ0=1\Phi=\phi_{0}=1, where the potential vanishes, and which leads to the action of an extremal black hole [67]. We find the JT gravity action (3.2), with Φ=ϕ0+ϕ\Phi=\phi_{0}+\phi and ϕ≪ϕ0\phi\ll\phi_{0}.

From the point of view of the two-dimensional background, ϕ0\phi_{0} is a topological term in the action and does not change the equations of motion. However, the dimensional reduction confers an interpretation to the dilaton as the area associated with points in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Let the wedge 𝒲\mathcal{W} be such that ð𝒲=∪iPi\eth\mathcal{W}=\cup_{i}P_{i} with {Pi}\{P_{i}\} a set of points in ℳ\mathcal{M}. It is associated with a (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional spherically symmetric wedge 𝒲^\hat{\mathcal{W}} in ℳ^\hat{\mathcal{M}} through dimensional reduction. Then,

A⁡(ð​𝒲^)4​G^=∑iΦ⁡(Pi)4​G.\frac{A(\eth\hat{\mathcal{W}})}{4\hat{G}}=\sum_{i}\frac{\Phi(P_{i})}{4G}. (A.5)

Thus, we impose

Φ≥0.\Phi\geq 0. (A.6)

This leads to the definition of an expansion parameter for lightrays in the two-dimensional background,

θ=1Φ​d​Φd​λ=Φ′Φ,\theta=\frac{1}{\Phi}\frac{d\Phi}{d\lambda}=\frac{\Phi^{\prime}}{\Phi}, (A.7)

where ′=dd​λ{}^{\prime}=\frac{d}{d\lambda} denotes differentiation with respect to an affine parameter λ\lambda along ∂+𝒲\partial^{+}\mathcal{W}.

Taking the derivative of (A.7) with respect to the affine parameter λ\lambda yields the two-dimensional Raychaudhuri equation:

θ′=Φ′′Φ−θ2.\theta^{\prime}=\frac{\Phi^{\prime\prime}}{\Phi}-\theta^{2}. (A.8)

From the classical equation of motion (3.7), one sees that Φ′′=−8​π​G​ki​kj​Ti​j\Phi^{\prime\prime}=-8\pi G~k^{i}k^{j}T_{ij} for any null vector kik^{i}, which is non-positive by the null energy condition. Since Φ\Phi is positive, one gets a two-dimensional version of the classical focusing theorem: θ′≤0\theta^{\prime}\leq 0. Equivalently, Eq. (A.8) can be obtained from the dimensional reduction of the Raychaudhuri equation in higher dimensions, with the metric ansatz (A.2). Indeed, let us consider a codimension-11 null congruence of curves in dd dimensions. For d>2d>2, the Raychaudhuri equation governing the evolution of its expansion scalar θ\theta reads:

d​θd​λ=−1d−2​θ2−ς^M​N​ς^M​N+ω^M​N​ω^M​N−R^M​N​kM​kN,\frac{d\theta}{d\lambda}=-\frac{1}{d-2}\theta^{2}-\hat{\varsigma}_{MN}\hat{\varsigma}^{MN}+\hat{\omega}_{MN}\hat{\omega}^{MN}-\hat{R}_{MN}k^{M}k^{N}, (A.9)

where ς^M​N\hat{\varsigma}_{MN} and ω^M​N\hat{\omega}_{MN} are the shear and twist tensors respectively, R^M​N\hat{R}_{MN} is the dd-dimensional Ricci tensor computed from the metric g^M​N\hat{g}_{MN}, and kMk^{M} a null vector orthogonal to the congruence. For an S​O​(d+1)SO(d+1)-symmetric congruence, compatible with the symmetry of the metric ansatz (A.2), kMk^{M} has no component along the (d−2)(d-2) compact dimensions, so that R^M​N​kM​kN=R^i​j​ki​kj\hat{R}_{MN}k^{M}k^{N}=\hat{R}_{ij}k^{i}k^{j}. Using the ansatz (A.2), one finds that

R^i​j=Ri​j−1Φ​∇i​∇jΦ+d−3d−2​1Φ2​∇iΦ​∇jΦ,\hat{R}_{ij}=R_{ij}-\frac{1}{\Phi}\nabla_{i}\nabla_{j}\Phi+\frac{d-3}{d-2}\frac{1}{\Phi^{2}}\nabla_{i}\Phi\nabla_{j}\Phi, (A.10)

where Ri​jR_{ij} is the two dimensional Ricci tensor computed from the metric gi​jg_{ij}. Using this relation, the dimensional reduction of the Raychaudhuri Eq. (A.9) gives (in absence of shear and twist):

d​θd​λ=Φ′′Φ−θ2−Ri​j​ki​kj.\frac{d\theta}{d\lambda}=\frac{\Phi^{\prime\prime}}{\Phi}-\theta^{2}-R_{ij}k^{i}k^{j}. (A.11)

Since in two dimensions the Ricci tensor is proportional to the metric tensor and kik^{i} is null, Ri​j​ki​kj=0R_{ij}k^{i}k^{j}=0, which indeed gives back Eq. (A.8).

Appendix B Sketch of the derivation of Eq. (4.27)

Here, we sketch the derivation of Eq. (4.27) from [9]. For a more comprehensive discussion, we refer the reader to that paper. It is understood that information-theoretic aspects of QFT are best described using operator algebras associated to subregions, and density matrices associated to subregions are in general ill-defined in the continuum limit [40]. Nevertheless throughout this section we assign density matrices to QFT subregions as a shortcut to obtain our result (one can imagine that this is possible after an appropriate regularization scheme). The final expression is writable in a manner which is regularization independent, and can be phrased in algebraic QFT language.

In [9], the shape deformation of the relative entropy was considered in a near-vacuum state of the type we discuss in Sec. 4. Let 𝒲\mathcal{W} denote a null-deformed Rindler wedges (as opposed to the main text, do not use tilde in this appendix to refer to the Rindler wedge since we are not worried about a mix up with the ball-shaped region). A wedge 𝒲\mathcal{W} is determined by a profile V⁡(ya)V(y^{a}) in Minkowski spacetime coordinates:

d​s2=−d​u​d​v+∑a=1d−2(d​ya)2,\displaystyle ds^{2}=-dudv+\sum_{a=1}^{d-2}(dy^{a})^{2}, (B.1)

where uu and vv are null coordinates and yay^{a} denotes the transverse direction. We can also consider a 11-parameter family of wedges 𝒲λ\mathcal{W}_{\lambda} with ∂λVλ≥0\partial_{\lambda}V_{\lambda}\geq 0.

Let us now denote by ρ𝒲\rho_{\mathcal{W}} and σ𝒲\sigma_{\mathcal{W}} the density matrices associated to 𝒲\mathcal{W} in a near-vacuum and the vacuum states respectively. An explicit near-vacuum density matrix ρ𝒲\rho_{\mathcal{W}} can be constructed as follows:

ρ𝒲=σ𝒲+δ​ρ𝒲,\displaystyle\rho_{\mathcal{W}}=\sigma_{\mathcal{W}}+\delta\rho_{\mathcal{W}}, (B.2)

where

δ​ρ𝒲=ϵ⁡(σ𝒲​Of+Of​σ𝒲).\displaystyle\delta\rho_{\mathcal{W}}=\epsilon(\sigma_{\mathcal{W}}O_{f}+O_{f}\sigma_{\mathcal{W}}). (B.3)

Here, ϵ≪1\epsilon\ll 1, and OfO_{f} is some smeared local Hermitian operator.

It is understood that the quantity appearing in the QNEC can be written in terms of shape deformation of the relative entropy in the following way [15, 47, 22]:

∂λδ​Srel​(ρ𝒲|σ𝒲)δ​V​(ya)|λ=2π⟨Tv​v⟩−∂λδ​Sren​(ρ𝒲)δ​V​(ya)|λ,\displaystyle\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm rel}(\rho_{\mathcal{W}}|\sigma_{\mathcal{W}})}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}=2\pi\langle T_{vv}\rangle-\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}(\rho_{\mathcal{W}})}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}, (B.4)

where ⟨Tv​v⟩\langle T_{vv}\rangle denotes expectation value in the near-vacuum state ρ\rho. We will compute the LHS of Eq. (B.4). For nearby density matrices, one has the following expansion (see e.g., Appendix B of [33]):

Srel(ρ𝒲|σ𝒲)=−∫−∞∞ds18​sinh2​(s+i​ϵ2)Tr[σ𝒲−1δρ𝒲σ𝒲i​s2​πδρ𝒲σ𝒲−i​s2​π]+O(δρ3).\displaystyle S_{\rm rel}(\rho_{\mathcal{W}}|\sigma_{\mathcal{W}})=-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}ds\frac{1}{8\sinh^{2}(\frac{s+i\epsilon}{2})}\Tr[\sigma_{\mathcal{W}}^{-1}\delta\rho_{\mathcal{W}}\sigma_{\mathcal{W}}^{\frac{is}{2\pi}}\delta\rho_{\mathcal{W}}\sigma_{\mathcal{W}}^{-\frac{is}{2\pi}}]+O(\delta\rho^{3}). (B.5)

Plugging in Eq. (B.3) and doing simple manipulations one arrives at:

Srel(ρ𝒲|σ𝒲)=−ϵ2∫−∞∞ds18​sinh2​(s+i​ϵ2)⟨Ofei​K​sOf⟩+O(ϵ3),\displaystyle S_{\rm rel}(\rho_{\mathcal{W}}|\sigma_{\mathcal{W}})=-\epsilon^{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}ds\frac{1}{8\sinh^{2}(\frac{s+i\epsilon}{2})}\langle O_{f}e^{iKs}O_{f}\rangle+O(\epsilon^{3}), (B.6)

where 2​π​K𝒲=log⁡σ𝒲−log⁡σ𝒲complement2\pi K_{\mathcal{W}}=\log\sigma_{\mathcal{W}}-\log\sigma_{\mathcal{W}^{\text{complement}}}, where 𝒲complement\mathcal{W}^{\text{complement}} denotes the causal complement of the wedge 𝒲\mathcal{W}, denotes the full modular Hamiltonian of the vacuum state associated with 𝒲\mathcal{W}. The expectation value in Eq. (B.6) is computed in the vacuum state. The full modular Hamiltonian can be explicitly written as the following boost-like expression:

K𝒲=2​π​∫−∞∞d​v​∫dd−2​ya​(v−V⁡(ya))​Tv​v​(u=0,v,ya).\displaystyle K_{\mathcal{W}}=2\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dv\int d^{d-2}y^{a}~(v-V(y^{a}))T_{vv}(u=0,v,y^{a}). (B.7)

It turns how that modular Hamiltonians of different cuts of the Rindler wedge are related like below:

e−i​K𝒲​s​e−i​K0​s=ei⁡(es−1)​∫d​ya​∫d​v​V​(ya)​Tv​v​(u=0,v,ya),\displaystyle e^{-iK_{\mathcal{W}}s}e^{-iK_{0}s}=e^{i(e^{s}-1)\int dy^{a}\int dv~V(y^{a})T_{vv}(u=0,v,y^{a})}, (B.8)

where K0K_{0} denotes the full modular Hamiltonian for the original Rindler wedge, i.e., one corresponding to V=0V=0. This relations allows us to compute the shape derivative in Eq. (B.4) explicitly from Eq. (B.6). Each derivative drops down factors of the averaged null energy operator ℰ⁡(ya)=∫−∞∞d​v​Tv​v​(u=0,v,ya)\mathcal{E}(y^{a})=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dv~T_{vv}(u=0,v,y^{a}) from the full modular Hamiltonian term, and we end up with:

∂λδ​Srel​(ρ𝒲|σ𝒲)δ​V​(ya)|λ=ϵ22∫dd−2y′a∫ds∂λVλ(y′a)⟨Ofℰ(ya)ℰ(y′a)ei​K𝒲λ​sOf⟩+O(ϵ3).\displaystyle\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm rel}(\rho_{\mathcal{W}}|\sigma_{\mathcal{W}})}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}=\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{2}\int d^{d-2}y^{\prime a}\int ds~\partial_{\lambda}V_{\lambda}(y^{\prime a})\langle O_{f}\mathcal{E}(y^{a})\mathcal{E}(y^{\prime a})e^{iK_{\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}}s}O_{f}\rangle+O(\epsilon^{3}). (B.9)

Note that the QNEC implies that the RHS is positive. Also, since the full modular Hamiltonian of any 𝒲\mathcal{W} annihilates the vacuum, we can write the above as:

∂λδ​Srel​(ρ𝒲|σ𝒲)δ​V​(ya)|λ=ϵ22∫dd−2y′a∫ds∂λVλ(y′a)⟨Ofℰ(ya)ℰ(y′a)Ofs⟩+O(ϵ3),\displaystyle\partial_{\lambda}\left.\frac{\delta S_{\rm rel}(\rho_{\mathcal{W}}|\sigma_{\mathcal{W}})}{\delta V(y^{a})}\right\rvert_{\lambda}=\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{2}\int d^{d-2}y^{\prime a}\int ds~\partial_{\lambda}V_{\lambda}(y^{\prime a})\langle O_{f}\mathcal{E}(y^{a})\mathcal{E}(y^{\prime a})O_{f_{s}}\rangle+O(\epsilon^{3}), (B.10)

where

Ofs=ei​K𝒲λ​s​Of​e−i​K𝒲λ​s\displaystyle O_{f_{s}}=e^{iK_{\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}}s}O_{f}e^{-iK_{\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}}s} (B.11)

is a modular-evolved OfO_{f} (simply a boost for 𝒲\mathcal{W} that are Rindler wedges).

Along with the condition ⟨Tv​v⟩ρ=0\langle T_{vv}\rangle_{\rho}=0 which we engineered in Sec. 4, Eq. (B.10) gives us Eq. (4.27).

Appendix C The generalized entropy perturbative expansion in the semiclassical regime, and the 𝑸Q term

As discussed in the introduction, Sec. 2, and Sec. 4, in the perturbatively semiclassical gravity regime we expect the following expansion for the generalized entropy:

Sgen​(𝒲)=c⁡(A⁡(ð​𝒲)4​ℓSd−2+⋯+Sren(1)+Q⁡(𝒲)),\displaystyle S_{\rm gen}(\mathcal{W})=c\left(\frac{A(\eth\mathcal{W})}{4\ell_{S}^{d-2}}+\cdots+S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}+Q(\mathcal{W})\right), (C.1)

where Q⁡(𝒲)Q(\mathcal{W}) denotes corrections that are o⁡(ℓS0)o(\ell_{S}^{0}) in the expansion. In this appendix, we study SgenS_{\rm gen} in an explicit theory in which we derive this ansatz for a simple example, including the lesser-studied QQ term in Eq. (C.1). We then present an argument for the order of magnitude of the QQ term in the setup of Sec. 4 (under Eq. (4.12)).

The particular class of theories in which we investigate this are dd-dimensional holographic brane-world theories (see [60, 61, 64, 39, 70, 46, 28, 55]). In fact, these are theories in which the proof of the rQFC was given in [63]. The theory has a perturbative semiclassical limit in which a holographic CFT is weakly coupled to gravity (in fact, the gravity is induced by the CFT). The (Euclidean) action of this theory can be computed holographically in terms of that of a AdSd+1 spacetime with an end-of-the-world brane with a specific tension (on which the brane-world theory lives). Explicitly:

log⁡Zbrane−world​[gi​j]\displaystyle\log Z_{\rm brane-world}[g_{ij}] =116​π​Gd+1​∫bulkdd​x​𝑑z​−G​(Gμ​ν​Rμ​ν+d⁡(d−1)ℓAdS2)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{16\pi G_{d+1}}\int_{\rm bulk}d^{d}xdz~\sqrt{-G}\left(G^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu}+\frac{d(d-1)}{\ell_{\rm AdS}^{2}}\right)
+18​π​Gd+1∫braneddx−g(K−T),\displaystyle+\frac{1}{8\pi G_{d+1}}\int_{\rm brane}d^{d}x~\sqrt{-g}(K-T), (C.2)

where Gμ​νG_{\mu\nu} and Rμ​νR_{\mu\nu} are the bulk metric and Ricci tensor respectively, xx denotes coordinates on the brane, and zz denotes the emergent bulk direction. Furthermore, KK is the extrinsic curvature of the brane, and T∝1/ℓAdST\propto 1/\ell_{\rm AdS} is the brane tension. The boundary conditions administered on the brane is:

Ki​j−K​gi​j=T​gi​j.\displaystyle K_{ij}-Kg_{ij}=Tg_{ij}. (C.3)

Our perturbative semiclassical theory lives on the brane with metric gi​jg_{ij}, and is dual to classical Einstein gravity in the bulk (i.e., Gd+1→0G_{d+1}\to 0 limit).3737 37 This setup is very similar to the way one defines the partition function of a holographic CFT with a cutoff in terms of AdS gravity with a “Dirichlet brane”. The main difference here is that instead of the usual Dirichlet boundary conditions, we administer the boundary condition (C.3) in the presence of an end-of-the-world brane. The fictitious cutoff surface is then replaced by a brane whose location is determined dynamically. This ends up having the effect of turning on gravity on the brane. To see that this indeed is a perturbative semiclassical theory, one can expand the action (C.2) in the limit of where the length scales on gi​jg_{ij} are much larger than ℓAdS\ell_{\rm AdS}. The result is (see e.g. [55]):

log⁡Zbrane−world​[gi​j]=116​π​Gd​∫branedd​x​−g\displaystyle\log Z_{\rm brane-world}[g_{ij}]=\frac{1}{16\pi G_{d}}\int_{\rm brane}d^{d}x\sqrt{-g} (gi​j​Ri​j+ℓAdS2​(curvature-squared terms)+⋯)\displaystyle\left(g^{ij}R_{ij}+\ell_{\rm AdS}^{2}(\text{curvature-squared terms})+\cdots\right)
+log⁡ZCFT​[gi​j]+o⁡(c​ℓAdS0),\displaystyle+\log Z_{\rm CFT}[g_{ij}]+o(c\ell_{\rm AdS}^{0}), (C.4)

where Ri​jR_{ij} is the intrinsic Ricci tensor on the brane, and

1Gd=ℓAdS(d−2)​Gd+1.\displaystyle\frac{1}{G_{d}}=\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}}{(d-2)G_{d+1}}. (C.5)

In Eq. (C.4), the ellipsis in the parenthesis denotes further higher curvature corrections suppressed by appropriate powers of ℓAdS\ell_{\rm AdS}. We see that ℓAdS\ell_{\rm AdS} acts as species scale in Eq. (C.4). In fact, holographic CFTs contain large number of matter fields. For example, in 𝒩=4\mathcal{N}=4 super Yang-Mills, we have:

ℓAdS3∝N2​G5.\displaystyle\ell_{\rm AdS}^{3}\propto N^{2}G_{5}. (C.6)

Combining Eqs. (C.6) and (C.5), we obtain ℓAdS2=c​G4\ell_{\rm AdS}^{2}=cG_{4}, where c∝N2c\propto N^{2}. More generally, we expect:

ℓAdSd−2=c​Gd,\displaystyle\ell_{\rm AdS}^{d-2}=cG_{d}, (C.7)

where cc is proportional to the effective number of matter fields in the holographic CFT. We conclude that the bulk AdS scale ℓAdS\ell_{\rm AdS} act as the brane-world theory’s species scale.

In this theory, the generalized entropy can be defined in a way analogous to the holographic entanglement entropy prescription for CFTs [28, 55]. That is, given a wedge on the brane, we can define:

Sgen​(𝒲)=A⁡(X)4​Gd+1,\displaystyle S_{\rm gen}(\mathcal{W})=\frac{A(X)}{4G_{d+1}}, (C.8)

where A⁡(X)A(X) is the area of the minimal bulk extremal surface which anchors to ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} on the brane (see Fig. 11). Similarly to action, we can expand this in the regime of small ℓAdS\ell_{\rm AdS} in terms of brane quantities, and obtain an expansion:

Sgen​(𝒲)=c⁡(A⁡(ð​𝒲)4​ℓAdSd−2+⋯+Sren(1)+Q⁡(𝒲)).\displaystyle S_{\rm gen}(\mathcal{W})=c\left(\frac{A(\eth\mathcal{W})}{4\ell_{\rm AdS}^{d-2}}+\cdots+S^{(1)}_{\rm ren}+Q(\mathcal{W})\right). (C.9)

Here, the ellipsis denotes higher curvature Dong entropy terms which depend on the geometry of ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W}, and QQ denotes corrections that are o⁡(ℓAdS)o(\ell_{\rm AdS}).

Let us derive this SgenS_{\rm gen} expansion in a specific example. Consider pure AdS dual to the brane-world in Minkowkski spacetime ηi​j\eta_{ij} and in the vacuum state. The bulk metric in standard Fefferman-Graham coordinates is:

d​s2=ℓAdS2z2​(d​z2+ηi​j​d​xi​d​xj),z≥ℓAdS.\displaystyle ds^{2}=\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}^{2}}{z^{2}}\left(dz^{2}+\eta_{ij}dx^{i}dx^{j}\right),~~~~~z\geq\ell_{\rm AdS}. (C.10)

This spacetime terminates at z=ℓAdSz=\ell_{\rm AdS} where the end-of-the-world brane sits.

Let (t,x,ya)(t,x,y^{a}) be standard Minkowski coordinates on the brane:

d​s2=−d​t2+d​x2+∑a=1d−2(d​ya)2.\displaystyle ds^{2}=-dt^{2}+dx^{2}+\sum_{a=1}^{d-2}(dy^{a})^{2}. (C.11)

Now, consider a “belt region” on the brane specified by:

{t=0,−L2≤x≤L2}.\displaystyle\{t=0,-\frac{L}{2}\leq x\leq\frac{L}{2}\}. (C.12)

We furthermore assume that the yay^{a} extent of the slab RR is much larger than LL, so is approximated as infinite for the purposes of the computation (see Fig. 10).

We would like to compute the corresponding generalized entropy (for the wedge which is the domain of dependence of this region) using the prescription (C.8). First, we must find the bulk extremal surface anchored to the slab. This can be specified by the embedding z⁡(x)z(x) which satisfies:

d​zd​x=z∗2​(d−1)−z2​(d−1)zd,\displaystyle\frac{dz}{dx}=\frac{\sqrt{z_{*}^{2(d-1)}-z^{2(d-1)}}}{z^{d}}, (C.13)

where z∗z_{*} is a constant and it marks the maximum value of zz that the bulk extremal surface reaches. It can be determined by solving:

L2=∫ℓAdSz∗d​z​zd−1z∗2​(d−1)−z2​(d−1).\displaystyle\frac{L}{2}=\int_{\ell_{\rm AdS}}^{z_{*}}dz\frac{z^{d-1}}{\sqrt{z_{*}^{2(d-1)}-z^{2(d-1)}}}. (C.14)

We can compute the area of the extremal surface:

Sgen=ℓAdSd−1​Rd−24​Gd+1∫−L/2L/2dx1+(d​zd​x)2zd−1=14​Gd+1[2​ℓAdSd−1d−2(RℓAdS)d−2+π​Γ​(2−d2​(d−1))(d−1)​Γ​(12​(d−1))ℓA​d​Sd−1(Rz∗)d−2].\displaystyle S_{\rm gen}=\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}^{d-1}R^{d-2}}{4G_{d+1}}\!\int_{-L/2}^{\,L/2}\!dx\;\frac{\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{dz}{dx}\right)^{2}}}{z^{d-1}}=\frac{1}{4G_{d+1}}\left[\frac{2\ell_{\rm AdS}^{d-1}}{d-2}\left(\frac{R}{\ell_{\rm AdS}}\right)^{d-2}+\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(\frac{2-d}{2(d-1)})}{(d-1)\Gamma(\frac{1}{2(d-1)})}\ell_{AdS}^{d-1}\left(\frac{R}{z_{*}}\right)^{d-2}\right]. (C.15)

From Eq.(C.14), one can solve for z∗z_{*} perturbatively in ℓS\ell_{S}. We find:

z∗=L⁡[a1+a2​(ℓAdSL)d+a3​(ℓAdSL)2​d+a4​(ℓAdSL)3​d−2+a5​(ℓAdSL)3​d+a6​(ℓAdSL)4​d−2+⋯],\displaystyle z_{*}=L\left[a_{1}+a_{2}\left(\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}}{L}\right)^{d}+a_{3}\left(\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}}{L}\right)^{2d}+a_{4}\left(\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}}{L}\right)^{3d-2}+a_{5}\left(\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}}{L}\right)^{3d}+a_{6}\left(\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}}{L}\right)^{4d-2}+\cdots\right], (C.16)

where aja_{j} are certain (derivable) dd-dependent numerical coefficients. We can then plug this into Eq. (C.15) to obtain the desired answer:

Sgen=c[2​Rd−24​ℓAdSd−2+b1(RL)d−2+b2(ℓAdSL)d(RL)d−2+b3(ℓAdSL)2​d(RL)d−2+b4(ℓAdSL)3​d(RL)d−2+b5(ℓAdSL)4​d−2(RL)d−2+⋯],\begin{split}S_{\rm gen}=&c\left[\frac{2R^{d-2}}{4\ell_{\rm AdS}^{d-2}}+b_{1}\left(\frac{R}{L}\right)^{d-2}+b_{2}\left(\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}}{L}\right)^{d}\left(\frac{R}{L}\right)^{d-2}+b_{3}\left(\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}}{L}\right)^{2d}\left(\frac{R}{L}\right)^{d-2}\right.\\ &\qquad\left.+b_{4}\left(\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}}{L}\right)^{3d}\left(\frac{R}{L}\right)^{d-2}+b_{5}\left(\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}}{L}\right)^{4d-2}\left(\frac{R}{L}\right)^{d-2}+\cdots\right],\end{split} (C.17)

where bjb_{j} are some dd-dependent numerical coefficients. The first term in Eq. (C.17) is the usual area term (A⁡(ð​𝒲)=2​Rd−2A(\eth\mathcal{W})=2R^{d-2}), and the second term is the renormalized von Neumann entropy. Note that there are no subleading SlocalS_{\rm local} contributions between the two because the local geometry of ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} is completely flat. Nevertheless, we see that there are non-trivial contributions at o⁡(ℓS)o(\ell_{S}). These are all part of the contributions which we have called QQ. We furthermore see that the contribution of QQ starts at O⁡(ℓAdSd)O(\ell_{\rm AdS}^{d}), consistent with the claim in Sec. 4 that the contribution of QQ to ∂λΘλ\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda} is o⁡(ℓS2​(d−2))o(\ell_{S}^{2(d-2)}).

The above is highly non-trivial evidence in support of the claim on the magnitude of QQ contribution to ∂λΘλ\partial_{\lambda}\Theta_{\lambda} (assumption in Eq. (4.13)). But the setting of the belt example is not equivalent to the setup of Sec. 4. Below, we sketch an argument in support of the claim in a more general setting. For a more general region and state on the brane, the computation of SgenS_{\rm gen} would involve solving for an extremal surface embedding surface (X¯r​(y,z),ya)(\bar{X}^{r}(y,z),y^{a}) for r=t,xr=t,x in the spacetime (see Fig. 11):

d​s2=ℓAdS2z2​(d​z2+gi​j​(z,x)​d​xi​d​xj),z>ℓAdS,\displaystyle ds^{2}=\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}^{2}}{z^{2}}\left(dz^{2}+g_{ij}(z,x)dx^{i}dx^{j}\right),z>\ell_{\rm AdS}, (C.18)

where

gi​j​(z,x)=ηi​j+zd​gi​j(d)​(x)+o⁡(zd).\displaystyle g_{ij}(z,x)=\eta_{ij}+z^{d}g^{(d)}_{ij}(x)+o(z^{d}). (C.19)

Eq. (C.19) comes from solving the Einstein field equations perturbatively in zz near z=0z=0. To find the brane metric, for example, we can evaluate gi​j​(z=ℓAdS,x)g_{ij}(z=\ell_{\rm AdS},x). Similarly to deriving the metric expansion (C.19), the near z=0z=0 expansion for X¯μ\bar{X}^{\mu} has been analyzed in [48, 3]. The result is:

X¯r​(ya,z)=(X(0))r​(ya)+z2​(X(2))r​(ya)+⋯+zd​δ​Srenδ​Xr​(ya),\displaystyle\bar{X}^{r}(y^{a},z)=(X^{(0)})^{r}(y^{a})+z^{2}(X^{(2)})^{r}(y^{a})+\cdots+z^{d}\frac{\delta S_{\rm ren}}{\delta X^{r}(y^{a})}, (C.20)

where (X(2))r​(ya)(X^{(2)})^{r}(y^{a}) depends only on the local geometry of ð​𝒲\eth\mathcal{W} on the brane. In the setup of Sec. 4, we can write this schematically as:

X¯r​(ya,z)=(X(0))r​(ya)+O⁡(z2R)+O⁡(ϵ​zdLd−1).\displaystyle\bar{X}^{r}(y^{a},z)=(X^{(0)})^{r}(y^{a})+O\left(\frac{z^{2}}{R}\right)+O\left(\epsilon\frac{z^{d}}{L^{d-1}}\right). (C.21)

Similarly, we can derive the following ansatz for z∗z_{*}, the turn around point of the extremal surface in the zz direction3838 38 Here we are assuming that the Fefferman-Graham expansion is valid in a neighborhood which includes the turn around point of X¯\bar{X}.

z∗=(z∗(0))+O⁡(ℓAdS2R)+O⁡(ϵ​ℓAdSdLd−1).\displaystyle z_{*}=(z_{*}^{(0)})+O\left(\frac{\ell_{\rm AdS}^{2}}{R}\right)+O\left(\frac{\epsilon\ell_{\rm AdS}^{d}}{L^{d-1}}\right). (C.22)

We then need to evaluate:

Sgen=1Gd+1​∫ℓAdSz∗d​z​∫dd−2​y​H¯​(ya,z),\displaystyle S_{\rm gen}=\frac{1}{G_{d+1}}\int_{\ell_{\rm AdS}}^{z_{*}}dz\int d^{d-2}y~\sqrt{\bar{H}(y^{a},z)}, (C.23)

where H¯​(ya,z)\bar{H}(y^{a},z) is the determinant of the intrinsic metric on the extremal surface. This can also be expaneded as follow:

H¯​(z,ya)=ℓSd−1zd−1​[f(0)​(z,y)+z2R​f(2)​(y,z)+ϵ​zdLd−1​f(d)​(y,z)+⋯].\displaystyle\sqrt{\bar{H}(z,y^{a})}=\frac{\ell_{S}^{d-1}}{z^{d-1}}\left[f^{(0)}(z,y)+\frac{z^{2}}{R}f^{(2)}(y,z)+\frac{\epsilon z^{d}}{L^{d-1}}f^{(d)}(y,z)+\cdots\right]. (C.24)

We need to explicitly compute:

1c​Sgen∝∫dd−2​y​∫ℓAdSz∗d​zzd−1​(f(0)​(z,y)+z2R​f(2)​(y,z)+ϵ​zdLd−1​f(d)​(y,z)+⋯),\displaystyle\frac{1}{c}S_{\rm gen}\propto\int d^{d-2}y\int_{\ell_{\rm AdS}}^{z_{*}}\frac{dz}{z^{d-1}}\left(f^{(0)}(z,y)+\frac{z^{2}}{R}f^{(2)}(y,z)+\frac{\epsilon z^{d}}{L^{d-1}}f^{(d)}(y,z)+\cdots\right), (C.25)

where for the prefactors we used the above-mentioned relation between Gd+1G_{d+1}, GdG_{d}, and ℓAdS\ell_{\rm AdS}, and cc.

We can analyze the perturbative expansion in ℓAdS\ell_{\rm AdS} of the integral (C.25). The terms in the integrand which blow up at z=0z=0, can be analyzed locally near the lower bound z=ℓAdSz=\ell_{\rm AdS} of the integral. For example, the first two terms give powers of ℓAdS2−d\ell_{\rm AdS}^{2-d} and ℓAdS4−d\ell_{\rm AdS}^{4-d} and will clearly have the form of a local integral in yay^{a}. These constitute the SlocalS_{\rm local} contributions in Eq. (C.9). To understand the (non-trivial) terms in QQ, we need to understand the perturbative contributions related to the upper bound z∗z_{*}. The leading order contribution from Eq. (C.22) gives an O⁡(1)O(1) contribution inside of the integral. This constitute the SrenS_{\rm ren} term in Eq. (C.9). Further corrections would be then suppressed by the same factors that corrections to z∗z_{*} are suppressed by in Eq. (C.22), namely O⁡(ℓAdS2/R)O(\ell_{\rm AdS}^{2}/R) and O⁡(ϵ​ℓAdSd/Ld−1)O(\epsilon\ell_{\rm AdS}^{d}/L^{d-1}) Both of these contributions in the context of Sec. 4 where R∼ℓAdS2−dR\sim\ell_{\rm AdS}^{2-d} become O⁡(ℓAdSd)O(\ell_{\rm AdS}^{d}). Furthermore, since ∂λΘ\partial_{\lambda}\Theta has an additional multiplicative factor of GdG_{d}, the conclusion is that the contribution of the QQ term satisfies O⁡(ℓAdS2​(d−1))O(\ell_{\rm AdS}^{2(d-1)}) at most and is therefore compatible with the assumption o⁡(ℓAdS2​(d−2))o(\ell_{\rm AdS}^{2(d-2)}) (see Eq. (4.13)).

Appendix D The ℰ×ℰ\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{E} OPE

As discussed in Sec. 4, the rQFC implies that δ≥0\delta\geq 0 in the following expression:

∫−∞∞d​s​e2​⟨O~f(1)​ℰ​(y~′a)​ℰ​(y~a)​O~fs(1)⟩=y~′→y~O⁡(|y~−y~′|−δ)\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}ds~e^{2}\langle\tilde{O}^{(1)}_{f}\mathcal{E}(\tilde{y}^{\prime a})\mathcal{E}(\tilde{y}^{a})\tilde{O}^{(1)}_{f_{s}}\rangle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{y}^{\prime}\to\tilde{y}}}{{=}}O(|\tilde{y}-\tilde{y}^{\prime}|^{{-\delta}}) (D.1)

The coincident limit y~′→y~\tilde{y}^{\prime}\to\tilde{y} is in particular controlled by the OPE of two ℰ\mathcal{E}’s. This is a less conventional OPE which involves light-ray operators (i.e., operators with support on null generators of the u~=0\tilde{u}=0 plane). See [49, 24] for a proper discussion of light-ray operators and their OPEs.

Here, we will simply write down the relevant OPE and explain it in some detail. For simplicity let us set of the transverse points to zero. Let |y~|=y~i​y~i|\tilde{y}|=\sqrt{\tilde{y}^{i}\tilde{y}_{i}}, and y^a=y~a/|y~|\hat{y}^{a}=\tilde{y}^{a}/|\tilde{y}|. The OPE takes the form (see [50, 49, 24]):

ℰ⁡(0)​ℰ​(y~a)=|y~|→0\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(0)\mathcal{E}(\tilde{y}^{a})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle|\tilde{y}|\to 0}}{{=}} ∑j,ncj,n|y~|δj,n−2​(d−1)y^a1⋯y^aj𝕆a1⋯aj(j,n)(0)+descendents of 𝕆(j,n)a1⋯aj,\displaystyle\sum_{j,n}c_{j,n}~|\tilde{y}|^{\delta_{j,n}-2(d-1)}\hat{y}^{a_{1}}\cdots\hat{y}^{a_{j}}~\mathbb{O}^{(j,n)}_{a_{1}\cdots a_{j}}(0)+\text{descendents of $\mathbb{O}^{(j,n)}_{a_{1}\cdots a_{j}}$}, (D.2)

where 𝕆(j,n)a1⋯aj\mathbb{O}^{(j,n)}_{a_{1}\cdots a_{j}} denotes a so-called light-ray operator with scaling dimension δj,n\delta_{j,n}, and transverse spin jj (see Fig. 12). Each operator 𝕆(j,n)a1⋯aj\mathbb{O}^{(j,n)}_{a_{1}\cdots a_{j}} is a non-local operator, and could be defined through smearing a pair local CFT operators in a certain way along a null geodesic. We will not cover the details of the light-ray OPE story here, but its structure (D.2) is sufficient for us to extract a certain bound on the spectrum δj,n\delta_{j,n}. Conveniently, the spectrum δj,n\delta_{j,n} could be described simply in terms of the spectrum of local CFT data, allowing us the ability to phrase the bound in terms of data of the local CFT spectrum. Let JJ denote total spin (as opposed to transverse spin jj), and let Δj,neven​(J)\Delta^{\text{even}}_{j,n}(J) be the analytically continued in JJ of the scaling dimension of the n-th Regge trajectory in the transverse spin jj sector. We then have [50, 49, 24]:

δj,n=\displaystyle\delta_{j,n}= Δj,neven​(J=3)−1,j=0,2,4.\displaystyle\Delta^{\text{even}}_{j,n}(J=3)-1,~~~j=0,2,4. (D.3)
δj,n=\displaystyle\delta_{j,n}= Δj=4,neven​(J=3+2​p)−1,j=4+2​p,(p∈ℤ+).\displaystyle\Delta^{\text{even}}_{j=4,n}(J=3+2p)-1,~~~j=4+2p,~(p\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}). (D.4)

It is easy to see from the OPE (D.2), that the leading Σ→0\Sigma\to 0 behavior of Eq. (4.27) is given by the smallest δj,n\delta_{j,n} which is contributing in the state. A particularly drastic way for the rQFC implication that δ≥0\delta\geq 0 in Eq. (D.1) to be violated is if the quantity δ0\delta_{0} defined as

δ0≡minn,j​δj,n.\displaystyle\delta_{0}\equiv\text{min}_{n,j}\delta_{j,n}. (D.5)

is such that in any state we obtain δ<0\delta<0. It is easy to see that for this not to happen we must have:

δ0≤2​(d−1).\displaystyle\delta_{0}\leq 2(d-1). (D.6)

In fact, Eq. (D.6) is equivalent to stating that:

lim|y~|→0ℰ⁡(0)​ℰ​(y~a)≠0,\displaystyle\lim_{|\tilde{y}|\to 0}\mathcal{E}(0)\mathcal{E}(\tilde{y}^{a})\neq 0, (D.7)

Note that this is a much weaker constraint than the one discussed in the body of the paper. In fact, it trivially follows from demanding that ℰ\mathcal{E} is non-zero as an operator.3939 39 We thank Raghu Mahajan for pointing this out..

Let us now investigate how close can δ0\delta_{0} get to 2(d-1) in a few simple cases. First, in the case of free theories, the leading Regge trajectory (n=1n=1) satisfies:

Δj=0,1even​(J)=d−2+J.\displaystyle\Delta^{\text{even}}_{j=0,1}(J)=d-2+J. (D.8)

Therefore, from Eq. (D.4) we have δj=0,n=1=d\delta_{j=0,n=1}=d, which satisfies the bound (D.6) with room to spare in d≥3d\geq 3.

Interestingly, we can obtain δ0=2​(d−1)\delta_{0}=2(d-1) in planar 𝒩=4\mathcal{N}=4 SU(N)(N) super Yang-Mills in the large t’Hooft coupling limit.4040 40 We thank David Simmons-Duffin for explaining to us the story of 𝒩=4\mathcal{N}=4 Super Yang-Mills. In the N→∞N\to\infty, limit, we can delineate the Regge trajectories of single and double-trace operators. It turns out that in the large t’Hooft coupling limit, the single-trace minj​Δj,1even​(J)\text{min}_{j}\Delta^{\text{even}}_{j,1}(J) can be arbitrarily increased for each JJ, but the leading double-trace trajectory satisfies minj​Δj,1even​(J)=4+J\text{min}_{j}\Delta^{\text{even}}_{j,1}(J)=4+J (approaching it from below in the N→∞N\to\infty limit) [43, 49]. Therefore, the double-trace trajectory leads to minj​δj,1=6\text{min}_{j}\delta_{j,1}=6, which saturates the bound (D.6) given d=4d=4.4141 41 For instance, one can consider the trajectory associated with the stress-tensor double-twist [T​T]J[TT]_{J}, which at large spin have twist (i.e., scaling dimension minus spin) τ⁡(J)=2​d+J−(J+4)=2​d−4\tau(J)=2d+J-(J+4)=2d-4. We then obtain Δ⁡(J=3)=τ⁡(J=3)+3=2​d−1\Delta(J=3)=\tau(J=3)+3=2d-1.
